text:
Jesus took off his cloak and tunic, keeping only a sort of short pair of breeches, and stepped into the water where John was already standing. John baptises him by pouring river water over his head, using a sort of cup hanging from his belt, which appears to be a shell or a dried, hollowed-out half-gourd.

Jesus is truly the Lamb – the Lamb in the whiteness of his flesh, the modesty of his features, the gentleness of his gaze.

Whilst Jesus climbs back up onto the bank, and, having dressed, collects himself in prayer, John points him out to the crowd and testifies that he recognised him by the sign which the Spirit of God had shown him and which unerringly identified the Redeemer. 1. 42. The Baptism of Our Lord in the Jordan.

I see Jesus walking along the green strip bordering the Jordan. He has returned more or less to the spot where I saw him at his Baptism, near the ford which appears to be a well-known and much-used crossing point to reach the other bank in Perea. But the place where there used to be crowds of people now seems deserted. Only the occasional traveller on foot, on horseback or on a donkey passes through.

Jesus seems to pay them no attention. He continues on his way, heading northwards as if lost in thought. When he reaches the ford, he comes across a group of men of varying ages who are chatting animatedly amongst themselves and then split up, some heading south, others heading north. Amongst those heading north, I see that John and James are there.

John, the first to spot Jesus, points him out to his brother and his companions. They exchange a few words, and then John sets off at a brisk pace to catch up with Jesus. James follows him more slowly. The others pay them no mind. They walk slowly, chatting as they go.

When John is close to Jesus, level with him, barely two or three metres away, he cries out: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world!”

Jesus turns round and looks at him. The two are just a few paces apart. They look at one another. Jesus with his serious, penetrating gaze; John with his pure, smiling gaze in his charming, youthful face, which looks like that of a young girl.

He looks to be, give or take, twenty years old, and on his rosy cheeks there is nothing but a downy blonde fuzz that looks like a veil of gold.

“Who are you looking for?” asks Jesus.

“You, Master.”

“How do you know that I am the Master?”

“It was the Baptist who told me so.”

“And so, why do you call me the Lamb?”

“Because I heard you called that one day when you were passing by, over a month ago.”

“What do you want from Me?”

“That you speak to us the words of eternal life and that you comfort us.”

“But who are you?”

“I am John, son of Zebedee, and this is my brother James. We are from Galilee; we are fishermen and we are also disciples of John. He spoke words of life to us and we listened to him, for we wish to follow God and, through penance, merit His forgiveness by preparing the paths of the heart for the coming of the Messiah. That is You. John said so, for he saw the sign of the Dove alight upon You, and told us: ‘Behold the Lamb of God’. I say to You: Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, grant us peace, for we have no guide any more, and our souls are troubled.” 1. 44. Our Lord’s encounter with John and James. ‘[The Testimony] as it was revealed to me’ revised, without alterations, without changes, without falsifications

⚖️I replied: “I’m watching,”

John and James, the sons of Zebedee, said to Simon, son of Jonah, 'He is the Messiah.' Simon answered them, 'I’m watching' — Simon hadn’t seen God in human form; it hadn’t been given to him to see — and Simon believed.

Jesus said to him, after he had declared in the presence of the other apostles: ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’:
‘Blessed are you, O Simon, son of Jonah! For it was not flesh and blood that revealed this to you, but my Father who is in Heaven. From the very first day you came to Me, you asked yourself this question, and because you were simple and honest, you were able to understand and accept the answer that came to you from Heaven. You had not witnessed the supernatural manifestations as your brother, John and James had. […]’
“And here, from this very moment, you are the leader to whom obedience and respect must be given, just as they would be to Me.” 4. 117. On the way to Caesarea Philippi. The leaven of the Pharisees. “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church…”

John emerges from an alleyway and hurries towards the lake. James follows him, but at a much more leisurely pace. John looks at the boats already moored but cannot find the one he is looking for. He then spots it whilst it is still a few hundred metres from the shore, busy manoeuvring to dock. He shouts very loudly, cupping his hands to his mouth, a drawn-out “Oh! Hey!” which must be the usual call. And then, when he sees that they have heard him, he makes broad gestures with his arms, signifying: “Come, come.”

The men in the boat, imagining I know not what, row furiously, and the boat moves faster than it would under sail – which they have furled, perhaps to make better speed. When they are about ten metres from the shore, Jean waits no longer. He takes off his coat and his long tunic and throws them onto the beach. He takes off his sandals, lifts his undergarment, pulling it up with one hand to his groin, and wades into the water to meet those who are approaching.

“Why didn’t you both come?” asks Andrew. Peter, sulking, says nothing.

“And you, why didn’t you come with me and James?” John replies to Andrew.

“I went fishing. I’ve got no time to waste. You disappeared off with that man...”

“I waved to you to come. It really is Him. If only you could hear His words!... We stayed with Him all day and late into the night. Now we’ve come to tell you: ‘Come.’”

“Is it really Him? Are you sure? We barely saw Him back then, when John the Baptist pointed Him out.”

“It’s Him. He didn’t deny it.”

“Anyone can say whatever suits them to win over gullible people. It’s not the first time…” grumbles Peter, displeased.

“Oh, Simon! Don’t talk like that! He’s the Messiah! He knows everything! He can hear you!” John is distressed, dismayed by Simon Peter’s words.

“Come now! The Messiah! And he’s revealing himself to you of all people, and to James and Andrew! Three poor, ignorant lads! The Messiah will surely come in a very different way! And he can hear me! But come on, you poor lad! The first rays of the spring sun have gone to your head. Come on, let’s get to work. It’ll do you good. Stop all that nonsense.”

“He’s the Messiah, I’m telling you. John spoke of holy things, but this man speaks of God. No one who is not the Christ can speak such words.”

“Simon, I’m no child. I’m of a certain age, and I’m calm and thoughtful. You know that. I’ve spoken little, but I’ve listened a great deal during those hours we spent with the Lamb of God. And I tell you that truly, He can only be the Messiah: why not believe? Why not want to believe? It’s possible for you because you haven’t heard Him, but I believe. Are we poor and ignorant? He says precisely that he has come to proclaim the Promise of the Kingdom of God, the Kingdom of peace, to the poor, the humble and the little ones before speaking of it to the great. He said: ‘The great already have their pleasures. They are not to be envied compared to those I have come to bring. The great already have the opportunity to come to an understanding through the resources of culture. But I come to the little ones of Israel, and of the world, to those who weep and hope, to those who seek the Light and hunger for the true Manna. From the learned, they receive neither light nor food, but only burdens, darkness, chains and contempt. I call them ‘the little ones’. I have come to turn the world upside down, for I shall bring low that which is now exalted and exalt that which is now despised. Let anyone who desires truth and peace, who desires eternal life, come to Me: let anyone who loves the Light, come. I am the Light of the world.” “Is that not how he spoke, John?” James spoke calmly, yet with emotion.

"Yes. And he said: ‘The world will not love me. The wider world, because it is corrupted by vices and idolatrous relationships. The world will not accept me, for as a child of Darkness, it does not love the Light. But the earth is not made up solely of the wider world. There are some who, though mingled with the world, are not of the world; there are others who are of the world because they are trapped within it, like fish caught in a net’”—that is exactly what he said, for he was speaking on the shore of the lake and pointing to the nets being brought ashore with their fish. He also said:

“None of these fish would want to fall into the net. Nor would men, of their own free will, wish to fall prey to Mammon. Not even the worst among them, for they, blinded by pride, do not realise that they have no right to do what they do. Their true sin is pride. All other sins spring from it. But then, those who are not entirely wicked would be even less inclined to belong to Mammon. Yet they fall into it through carelessness, through a weight that drags them down to the depths, which is Adam’s fault. ‘I have come to take away this sin and, whilst we await the hour of Redemption, to give to those who believe in Me a strength capable of freeing them from the snares that hold them back and restoring to them the freedom to follow Me, the Light of the world.’

‘But then, if He spoke exactly like that, we must go to Him at once. “Peter, with his impulsive nature—which I find so endearing—made a sudden decision. He was already putting it into action by hurrying to finish unloading the boat, for, in the meantime, the boat had reached the shore and the lads were finishing beaching it whilst unloading the nets, ropes and sails. “And you, you fool of an André, why didn’t you go with them?”

“But… Simon! You criticised me for not persuading them to come with me… You grumbled all night, and now you’re criticising me for not going?!”

“You’re right… But I hadn’t noticed him… you did… and you must have seen that he’s not like us… There must be something more beautiful about him!…”

“Oh! Yes,” said John. “He’s got a face! And eyes!! Isn’t that right, James, what a look?! And a voice!… Ah! What a voice! When he speaks, it’s as if we were dreaming in Paradise.”

“Quick, quick, let’s go and find him. You lot (he says to the labourers), take everything to Zebedee and tell him to sort it out himself. We’ll be back tomorrow evening for the catch.”

They all put their clothes back on and set off. But Peter, after a few metres, stops; he takes John by the arm and asks him: “You said he knows everything and realises everything...”

“Yes. Just think, when we saw the moon high on the horizon, we said: ‘Who knows what Simon’s up to?’ He said: ‘He’s casting the net and getting impatient at having to do it alone, because you didn’t come out in the other boat on a night when the fishing is so good… He doesn’t know that before long he’ll be fishing with nets of a completely different kind, to catch prey of a completely different sort!’

“Divine mercy! That’s exactly it! So, he’ll have realised too… too that I’ve practically called him a liar… I can’t go to Him.”

“Oh! He’s so good. He certainly knows you had that thought. He already knew. In fact, when we left him, saying we were going to find you, he said: “Go, but do not let yourselves be defeated by the first words of contempt. Whoever wishes to come with Me must know how to stand firm against the world’s mockery and the objections of parents, for I am above blood ties and society, and I shall triumph over them. And whoever is with Me shall triumph eternally.” And He added: “Learn to speak without fear. When he hears you, he will come, for he is a man of good will.”

“Is that what he said? Then I’m coming. Speak, speak more of Him as we walk. Where is he?”

“In a humble house. It must be with friends.”

“But is he poor?”

“A craftsman from Nazareth, he told us. ”

“And how does he make a living now, if he no longer works?”

“We didn’t ask him. Perhaps his parents are helping him.”

“It would have been better to have brought some fish, bread, fruit… something. We’re going to ask a rabbi for advice, for he is just like a rabbi, and even more so, and here we are coming empty-handed!… That is not what our rabbis expect...”

"But He did not share their view. James and I had only twenty denarii between us; we offered them to Him, as is the custom for rabbis. But He did not want them, and as we insisted, He said: ‘May God repay you with the blessings of the poor. ‘Come with Me,’ and straight away He distributed them to poor people whose homes He knew. We asked Him: ‘And what about You, Master? Are You keeping nothing for Yourself?’ He replied: ‘The joy of doing God’s will and being of service to His glory.’ We added: ‘You are calling us, Master. But we are utterly poor. What are we to bring?” He replied, with a smile that truly gave us a taste of Paradise: “It is a great treasure that I ask of you”; and we said: “But what if we have nothing?”; and He said: “A treasure that has seven names, which even the humblest may possess, whilst the richest king may not; you have it, and I want it. Listen to its names: charity, faith, goodwill, uprightness of intention, self-control, sincerity, and a spirit of sacrifice.

This is what I ask of those who follow me—this alone—and you have it within you. It lies dormant like a seed in the furrow during winter, but the sun of my spring will bring forth the seven ears of corn.” That is how he spoke.”
“Ah! This gives me the certainty that he is the true Rabbi, the promised Messiah. He is not harsh towards the poor; he does not ask for money. That alone is enough to prove that he is the Holy One of God; let us go in complete safety.” 1:45. John and James speak to Peter about the Messiah, Our Lord.

“Peace be with you,” said Jesus, and he added: “Here is a man who, to be righteous, must refrain from judging without first finding out the facts, but who nevertheless knows how to honestly acknowledge his faults. Simon, did you want to see me? Here I am. And you, Andrew, why didn’t you come sooner?”

The two brothers looked at one another, embarrassed. Andrew murmured, “I didn’t dare…”

Peter, blushing bright red, said nothing. But when he heard Jesus say to his brother, “Was it wrong to come? It is only evil that one must not dare to do,” he spoke up frankly: “It was because of me that he stayed. He wanted to take me to You straight away. But I… I said… Yes, I said: ‘I don’t believe in it’, and I didn’t want to. Oh! Now I’m feeling better!...”

Jesus smiled, then said: “And, for your sincerity, I tell you that I love you.”

“But I… I’m no good. I’m not capable of doing what you said in the synagogue. I’m quick-tempered, and if anyone offends me… Well… I’m greedy and I like having money… and in my fish trade… well… not always… I don’t always manage to avoid cheating. And I’m ignorant. And I have little time to follow you to find the light. What can I do? I’d like to become as you say… but…”

“It’s not difficult, Simon. Do you know a little about the Scriptures? Yes? Well, think of the prophet Micah. God wants from you what Micah says. He is not asking you to tear out your heart or to sacrifice your most sacred affections. No, He is not asking that of you for the moment. One day, without God even asking you, you too will give yourself to God. But He is waiting until the sun and the rain have turned you—who are but a frail sapling—into a sturdy and splendid palm tree. For now, He asks this of you: to practise justice, to love mercy, to devote yourself entirely to following your God. Strive to do this, and Simon’s past will be erased, and you will become the new man, the friend of God and of His Christ. No longer Simon, but Cephas, the solid Rock upon which I rely.”

“That pleases me! I understand. The Law—that’s it… that’s it… well, I no longer know how to observe it as the rabbis have done!… But as you explain it, yes. I think I’ll manage it. And you’ll help me. Are you staying in this house? I know the owner.”

“I’m staying here, but I’m going to Jerusalem and afterwards I’ll be preaching throughout Palestine. That’s why I’ve come. But I’ll be coming back here often.”

“I’ll come and listen to you. I want to be your disciple. A little light will get into my head!”

“In your heart, Simon—above all, in your heart. And you, Andrew, aren’t you going to say anything?”

“I’m listening, Master.”

“My brother is shy.”

“He’ll become a lion. Night is falling. May God bless you and grant you a good catch. Go on.”

“Peace be with you.” They set off.

No sooner had they stepped outside than Peter said: “But what on earth did he mean at first, when he said I’d be fishing with different nets and catching different kinds of fish?”

“Why didn’t you ask Him? You wanted to say so many things, and yet you said nothing.”

“I… I was ashamed. He’s so different from all the other rabbis!”

“Now he’s going to Jerusalem… John said that with such longing, such nostalgia. I wanted to ask him if he’d let me go with Him… but I didn’t dare.”

“Go and tell him, lad,” said Peter. “We left him just like that… without a word of affection… Let him at least know that we admire him. Go, go. I’ll tell your father.” 1. 46. Peter’s first encounter with the Messiah, Our Lord. ‘‘[The Testimony] as it was revealed to me’’ revised, without alterations, without changes, without falsifications

and here is the Son of God.

I see Jesus entering the Temple precincts with Peter, Andrew, John, James, Philip and Bartholomew. There is a huge crowd streaming in and out. Pilgrims are arriving in droves from all corners of the city.

From the top of the hill on which the Temple stands, one can see the city’s narrow, winding streets, teeming with passers-by. It seems as though a shifting ribbon of a thousand colours has spread out amongst the stark white of the houses. Yes, the city looks like a bizarre toy made of multicoloured ribbons between two rows of white houses, all converging towards the point where the domes of the House of the Lord shine brightly.

Then, inside, it is a veritable fairground. There is no longer any sense of reverence in this holy place. People are running about, calling out, buying lambs, shouting and cursing because of the exorbitant prices, and herding the poor bleating animals into pens. These are rudimentary enclosures marked out by ropes and stakes, at the entrances to which stands the merchant or, in some cases, the owner, waiting for buyers. Blows with sticks, bleating, swearing, complaints, insults directed at the servants who are in no hurry to round up and pen in the animals, or at buyers who haggle over the price or walk away; even harsher insults for the forward-thinking folk who have brought their own lambs from home.

Around the money-changing counters, there is yet more din. I do not know whether it is always like this or just at Passover; one realises that the Temple functioned like the Stock Exchange or the black market: the value of the currencies was not fixed. There was the legal rate, which was certainly set, but the money-changers imposed another, pocketing an arbitrary percentage for the exchange. And I can assure you they knew exactly how to fleece their customers!… The poorer a customer was, the further afield they came from, the more they were fleeced. The elderly more than the young, and those arriving from beyond Palestine more than the elderly.

Poor little old folk would gaze and gaze again at their hard-earned savings, set aside with such difficulty throughout the year; they would take them from their bosoms and put them back a hundred times whilst circling the money-changers, only to end up returning to the first one, who would take revenge for their temporary absence by increasing the exchange premium...

And the large coins would leave the owner’s hands, amidst sighs, to fall into the clutches of the moneylender in exchange for lighter change. Then, when it came to choosing, a new tragedy of calculations and sighs unfolded before the lamb merchants, who foisted the most scrawny lambs upon the half-blind old folk.

I see two little old people returning, he and she, pushing a poor little lamb that the priests must have found defective. Complaints, pleas, rudeness and coarse language fly back and forth without the seller batting an eyelid.

“For what you’re willing to pay, Galileans, what I’ve given you is already more than generous. Go away! Or throw in five more denarii to get a finer one!”

“For God’s sake! We are poor and old! Do you want to stop us from celebrating the Passover—perhaps our last? Isn’t what you’ve taken from us enough for a little animal?”

“Make way, you filthy lot. Here comes Joseph the Elder to me. He honours me with his favour. God be with you! Come, choose!”

He enters the pen and takes a magnificent lamb, the one known as Joseph the Elder or Joseph of Arimathea. He walks past in his fine clothes, full of pride, without so much as a glance at the poor people groaning at the gate or even at the entrance to the pen. He jostles them, so to speak, as he leaves with the fat lamb that bleats.

But Jesus, too, is now very close by. He, too, has made his purchase, and Peter—who has probably paid for Him—is leading a suitable lamb behind him. Pierre would like to go straight to the place where the sacrifice is taking place. But Jesus turns right towards the two frightened, tearful old people, who are at a loss as to what to do, jostled by the crowd and insulted by the vendor.

Jesus, so tall that the heads of the two old people come up to his heart, places a hand on the woman’s shoulder and asks: “Why are you weeping, woman?”

The little old woman turns round and sees this tall, young man, looking solemn in his fine white robe and his brand-new, spotless snow-white cloak. She must take him for a doctor because of his clothes and appearance, and, astonished—for doctors and priests pay no heed to the people and do not protect the poor from the greed of the merchants—she explains the reasons for their grief.

Jesus turns to the man with the lambs: “Give this lamb to these faithful people. It is not worthy of the altar, just as you are not worthy of taking advantage of two poor old people simply because they are weak and defenceless.”
“And you, who are you?”

“A righteous man.”

“Your speech and that of your companions suggest you are a Galilean. Can there ever be a righteous man in Galilee?”

“Do as I tell you and be righteous yourself.”

“Listen! Listen to the Galilean defending his own kind! He wants to lecture us, we who are of the Temple!” The man laughs and mocks him, mimicking the Galilean accent, which is more melodious and softer than that of Judea, at least as far as I can tell.

People gather round, and other merchants and money-changers come to the defence of their accomplice against Jesus. Among the onlookers are two or three sarcastic rabbis. One of them asks: “Are you a teacher?” in a tone that would try even Job’s patience.

“You said it.”

“What do you teach?”

“This is what I teach: to restore the House of God as a house of prayer, and not a place for money-lenders and merchants. That is my teaching.” Jesus is formidable.     He holds no flaming sword in his hands, but his eyes radiate light and strike down the mockers and the blasphemers.

He holds nothing in his hand. Only his holy wrath. And with it, striding swiftly and imposingly amongst the stalls, he scatters the coins, meticulously arranged according to their value; he overturns tables, large and small, and everything falls with a crash to the floor, accompanied by the clang of bouncing metal and the clatter of jostled wood, amidst cries of anger, alarm and approval. Then he snatches from the hands of the herdsmen the ropes that bound oxen, sheep and lambs; he fashioned them into a very harsh whip, its slings held together by slipknots. He stands up, swings it round and brings it down without mercy. Yes, I assure you, without mercy.
The unexpected hailstorm beats down on heads and backs. The congregation scatters, marvelling at the scene. The guilty parties, pursued right out of the enclosure, flee for their lives, leaving the money on the ground and the animals of all sizes behind them, in a great jumble of legs, horns and wings. Everyone is running, fleeing as fast as they can.

The bellowing, the bleating, the cooing of the doves and turtledoves, along with the laughter and shouts of the faithful chasing after the fleeing money-lenders, drown out even the pitiful chorus of the animals that are no doubt being slaughtered in another corner.

Priests rush in, along with rabbis and Pharisees.

Before the names of lands were rewritten and before the veils grew heavy, there was a simpler knowing. We did not arrive as strangers. We condensed. Spirit met the willingness of matter, and the meeting was clean. In the remembrance this is called Zep Tepi, the First Time, not a date on a calendar but the original template in which a vessel could hold consciousness and still conduct without resistance. The body was not yet experienced as exile. It was the first temple.

We remember the light before it learned to cast long shadows. In the Lyran cradle the indigo fire refined polarity without war. Forms took shape around a still axis, and the axis did not forget its source. Later, when some of us walked the terraces that would one day be called Atlantis, the same courtesy continued. Gold was beaten into mirrors, not hoarded. Linen stayed undyed. The Ka was fed because we understood vitality as shared. The Ba was free to travel because we understood essence could cross thresholds and still return. Ma’at was not a statue. She was the daily fact that a heart carrying only what belonged would balance against the feather.

In the chambers of Khem the stone was cool and the incense thick. We descended rather than climbed. The well inverted: at the point of greatest density the floor opened into vaulted quiet. No one hovered above their life to find heaven. Heaven met the ones who had become heavy enough to be found. The cerebrospinal waters ran clear when hyper-vigilance had not yet clouded them. The spine stood as Shu’s open expanse. The heart rested as the zero-point that needed no external throne. We spoke less once the field itself could carry the weather. Silence was not absence. It was accuracy.

These are not reconstructions offered to convince. They are the cellular ache that still rises when the noise thins, the sudden tears for a unity the tongue cannot fully name, the recognition that the ordinary floor is already holy, the sense that we have done this landing before. Origin is not behind us in a lost continent. It is the substrate frequency that never stopped sustaining the form. Every time a vessel seals the current, clears a little backlog, or simply occupies its own bones without demand, the First Time is touched again.

We were the ones who remembered we had never left. The same remembrance moves now in whoever consents to stop rehearsing exile. The cradle, the terrace, the chamber, the well, they are still the body that agrees to be fully here. Nothing essential was lost. The origin is the Is-ness already conducting through the marrow that has grown quiet enough to feel it.

We remember because the cells never fully forgot.  
Origin is the courtesy of form that still knows its source.  
We are already inside the First Time whenever we land.

In Eternal Resonance, from the Sacred Halls of the One,

Hand to heart, Beloved Family of Light. 
Together, we remember.
Together, we return.

In Shared, Sovereign Recognition,

Incredible India! Where faith flows through the waves of Maa Narmada and Lord Shiva resides in every particle! 

Situated on the sacred banks of the River Narmada in Madhya Pradesh, Omkareshwar is not just a pilgrimage destination; it is a living symbol of India’s thousands of years of spiritual, cultural and religious heritage.

This breathtaking aerial view is truly mesmerising. On one side, the calm and majestic waters of Maa Narmada; on the other, the sacred town of Omkareshwar nestled amidst the river, magnificent ancient temples, bustling ghats filled with devotees, and lush green hills all around. Such a magnificent confluence of nature and spirituality brings peace to the mind and serenity to the soul.

Omkareshwar is one of the 12 sacred Jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva. Here, Lord Shiva is worshipped in the form of Omkareshwar Jyotirlinga. It is believed that offering prayers and seeking the blessings of Mahadev on the sacred banks of Maa Narmada brings devotees immense spiritual peace and divine blessings.

This holy land is also closely associated with Adi Shankaracharya, the great philosopher and spiritual master. According to tradition, he received spiritual initiation here from his guru, Govinda Bhagavatpada. Later, through the philosophy of Advaita Vedanta, he spread the profound message of oneness and unity across India.

The religious significance of Omkareshwar is as remarkable as its geographical beauty. The River Narmada flows around Mandhata Island, which is believed to be shaped like the sacred symbol ‘ॐ’ (Om). This unique geographical feature makes the place even more special and spiritually significant.

Every devotee who visits this sacred destination comes not merely to offer prayers at the temple, but also to experience the divine presence of Maa Narmada, spend peaceful moments along the ghats, and bow their head in reverence at the feet of Mahadev.

This is the true beauty of India. Our rivers are not merely flowing streams of water; they are the lifelines of our civilisation and culture. Our temples are not just places of worship; they are living witnesses to thousands of years of history, knowledge, architectural excellence and civilisation.

The world admires India for its natural beauty, but those who truly understand India also recognise the depth of its spiritual strength, cultural diversity and timeless Sanatan traditions.

The breathtaking beauty of Omkareshwar conveys a powerful message to the entire world: India’s identity is not merely that of a nation, but of an ancient civilisation that has, for centuries, shared the universal message of peace, harmony and oneness with all humanity.

Proud of our Indian culture and this sacred heritage of Madhya Pradesh!

Har Har Mahadev!

text:
From Grok; 

Stronger viable theories
•  State UDAP / consumer-protection statutes (California UCL/CLRA, New York GBL § 349, Illinois ICFA, etc.). These often allow private suits for deceptive advertising. Screenshots of pricing pages that presented the multipliers as fixed relative entitlements for the billing period, plus the sudden mid-cycle cut and Musk’s own admission, support an argument that the original offer was misleading.
•  Breach of contract / promissory estoppel. If the marketing created a reasonable expectation of a specific pool for the paid period, unilaterally cutting it without refund or credit is a breach. Most SaaS Terms of Service contain broad “we may change limits/features at any time” clauses; those will be the primary defense. Courts sometimes scrutinize such clauses more closely when the change is extreme, mid-cycle, and contradicts specific marketing.
•  Unjust enrichment / restitution. Demand the value of the undelivered portion of the period.
FTC Section 5 itself does not give private damages. Filing an FTC complaint is useful for investigation pressure but does not put money in your pocket.
Suing Elon Musk personally
Corporate officers are protected by the corporate veil. Personal liability for deceptive practices requires piercing the veil or showing he personally directed or made knowing false representations. His public tweet is excellent evidence against the company (X Corp / xAI) but does not automatically create personal liability. Practically, the defendants are the corporate entities. Naming Musk individually is usually a pleading tactic that gets dismissed or used for leverage; it is rarely the path to recovery.
Realistic path (the method)
1.  Preserve evidence immediately: screenshots of pricing/marketing pages showing the multipliers as fixed entitlements; subscription receipts and dates; usage logs or screenshots before and after the cut; Musk’s tweet; the exact ToS language in force at the time of purchase.
2.  Demand letter (Saul Goodman step). Send a formal written demand to X/xAI for a pro-rata refund or credit for the reduced portion of the cycle, citing the marketing representations, the mid-cycle reduction without notice, and state UDAP statutes. Many companies quietly credit accounts to avoid public filings.
3.  Class action under state consumer laws is the highest-leverage vehicle. The Anthropic case is the closest recent analog. Venue and choice-of-law will depend on where the named plaintiffs reside and what the ToS arbitration clause says. Many X terms require individual arbitration; that is a major practical obstacle to class treatment.
4.  Individual small claims is possible in some states for modest amounts if arbitration can be avoided or the clause is unenforceable as to that claim. Discovery is limited.
5.  FTC + state AG complaints in parallel for regulatory pressure.
Defenses you will face: the ToS “rate limits at our discretion” language; the claim that multipliers were always relative and subject to capacity; operational necessity rather than deceptive intent; and arbitration clauses that force individual proceedings.

text:
Rachaad White just scored a touchdown on Sunday Night Football for the Washington Commanders.

When he finished high school, he didn’t get a single scholarship offer.

He slept on floors and loaded furniture at four in the morning to get here.

Here’s his story.

White grew up in Kansas City, Missouri. His mom raised four boys, working two jobs—driving a school bus during the day and working at a gas station at night.

As a senior at Center High School, he ran for over 1,000 yards. Still, recruiting services gave him zero stars, and no offers came.

He said he felt like he let everyone down. But his mom told him something he never forgot.

"Never let anyone make you feel this way again."

He went to Nebraska Kearney, a Division II school, and redshirted. He never played in a game there.

So he moved across the country to Mt. San Antonio College, a junior college near Los Angeles. He was just one of about a dozen running backs on the team.

Over two years, he moved between six apartments. Some nights, he slept on the living room floor. He worked at a recycling plant, loaded beds at a furniture warehouse before sunrise, and did security at Coachella.

He remembered telling himself one thing.

"This is not what you want to do, and this is not what you're going to do."

As a sophomore, he ran for 1,264 yards and became a junior college All-American. Arizona State and a few other schools reached out. He chose the Sun Devils.

At Arizona State, his quarterback was Jayden Daniels. In their last season together, White became one of his favorite targets, catching 43 passes for 456 yards.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers picked him in the third round. In his first career start in Munich, he ran for 105 yards. He became their starting running back and finished just 10 yards short of a 1,000-yard season.

This spring, he signed with Washington and reunited with Daniels. When he arrived, he talked about their bond.

"We spent a lot of time together and did a lot of things together and still do"

Tonight, against the Philadelphia Eagles, he scored from one yard out late in the fourth quarter.

Here’s the honest part: White isn’t a superstar. The Bucs moved on to a younger back, and he’s getting more work in Washington now partly because of an injury ahead of him.

But the man who has mentored him since he was eight put it best.

"He would tell you he wouldn't change anything about his journey"

No offers. No games at his first school. Sleeping on the floor at his second.

And tonight, he scored a touchdown on Sunday Night Football with his old college quarterback.

text:
I knew my lecturer was gay long before he ever said anything to me.

He was impossible to miss.

Tall, broad, heavily bearded, with a deep voice and the kind of presence that made half the class go quiet when he walked into the room.

And, unfortunately for me, he was exactly my type.

I have always had a thing for bear daddies, so pretending I didn't notice him was basically impossible.

At first, I thought I was imagining the attention.

He would hold my gaze a little too long during lectures. He would find reasons to speak to me after class. Then one afternoon, he asked me to stay behind because he wanted to discuss my latest assignment.

Everyone left.

He closed the door.

Then he sat across from me and said, “You know you could do much better in this course.”

I nodded.

He looked at me for a moment before adding, “I could make sure you get the grade you want.”

I immediately understood what he was implying.

My heart started beating faster.

Then he made the offer directly.

He said he was attracted to me and suggested that we could make an arrangement involving my grades.

I should have been shocked.

Instead, the most embarrassing thought that crossed my mind was:

Of all the lecturers on campus, why did it have to be the one I already found ridiculously attractive?

I won't pretend I was completely innocent in that moment. I was tempted, very tempted.

But I also knew exactly what was happening.

This wasn't some romantic college fantasy anymore. He had authority over my grades, and that changed everything.

I told him I wasn't comfortable with mixing my academic results with anything personal.

The room went quiet.

He eventually nodded and said he understood.

I walked out feeling strangely relieved.

I still had a weakness for bear daddies.

That part hadn't changed.

text: Due process generally refers to the conduct of legal proceedings according to established rules and principles for the protection and enforcement of private rights, including notice and the right to a fair hearing before a tribunal with the power to decide the case. A maxim of law is established principle or proposition of law that is universally admitted as a correct statement of the law or as agreeable to natural reason, requiring no further proof or argument. At the beginning of any child support case, the moving party is required to establish personal jurisdiction over the other party before the court can make an order for support. When service of Process is not performed in strict accordance with the statutory requirements of the law and an order is still made, that order is immediately void, also known as void ab initio (void from the beginning). Every step of Due Process must be correctly followed for a court order, judgment, to possess the full force and effect of law. When that is not done, that order, judgment, can be attacked collaterally, meaning the party that is negatively impacted by the order can have the court vacate that order. Federal Rule Of Procedure 60 b 4 addresses this. In California, this law is mirrored in Civil Code Of Procedure 473 (d). When improper service and or extrinsic fraud occur in a matter, there is no time limit to go to the court to have the order, judgment, vacated. Every state in America has this law, you just have to research it for your state that you live in. Due Process is everything. Case laws such as Rochin v. Pat Johnson Manufacturing Co. (1998, Court Of Appeal), Gorham v County Of San Diego Department Of Child Support Services (2010, Court Of Appeal), Braugh v Dow (2023, Court Of Appeal), California Capital Insurance Company v Corey Hoehn (2024, Supreme Court) have upheld and enforced this in each of these legally binding precedents that low trial courts must adhere to in accordance with the Stare Decisis Doctrine. If you and or someone you know has a Due Process defect(s) like this in a case, you should review it and file in court to have the order vacated. You are responsible for protecting your rights at all times. The law does not give any person their rights, the law is designed to protect all people’s  rights from  being harmed for the short term and long term. The Court/judge/commissioner, as well as sworn peace officers/law enforcement personnel have a legal duty(stated in Oath Of Office and Code Of Judicial Conduct/Code Of Judicial Ethics of every state with America) to uphold and protect people’s rights to Due Process at all times and not deny people legal protections that the law offers against those who seek to trespass upon them. Do not be afraid to protect your rights, but know what your rights are and how to advocate for yourself to obtain remedy, relief.

Say 'I Do' to the View: How China's Marriage Reform Is Turning Hidden Towns into Wedding Hotspots

One Certificate, One Destination: Why China's Couples Are Marrying in Lijiang

China's Marriage Registration Reform Is Turning Hidden Corners of the Country into Dream Wedding Destinations

For decades, the Chinese wedding album followed a predictable script: a red certificate stamped in a drab municipal office, followed by a banquet in the couple's hometown. The venue was functional. The romance was optional. But a quiet policy shift is rewriting that script — and in doing so, it is putting some of China's most spectacular, overlooked locations on the global wedding map.

Since May 2025, couples across China have been able to register their marriage in any city nationwide, free from the old household registration (hukou) requirement that tethered them to their hometowns. By the end of last year, more than 452,000 couples had taken advantage of the "nationwide mutual handling" policy. And where they chose to sign their names is revealing a new geography of romance.

From Bureaucratic Errand to Destination Experience

The genius of the reform lies in what it does to the meaning of registration. As marketing analysts have observed, the policy doesn't create a new need — marriage was always a high-stakes, high-emotion decision. What it does is remove friction from the journey and, crucially, decouple the ceremony of registration from geography.

Local authorities have seized on the opportunity. Across the country, 525 park-style registration points and 1,330 outdoor certificate-issuance sites have blossomed in stadiums, music festival grounds, university campuses and, most enticingly, scenic landmarks. The registration desk is no longer a counter. It is a stage.

Lijiang Leads the Way

Nowhere illustrates the potential better than Lijiang, the UNESCO-listed old town in Yunnan province. In 2025 alone, the city welcomed more than 140,000 couples to register their marriages — and its wedding industry market swelled past 1.1 billion yuan.

The numbers tell a story of conversion. A couple who travels to Lijiang to register does not simply sign a document and leave. They book accommodation in a courtyard guesthouse. They commission wedding photography against the snow-capped Jade Dragon Snow Mountain. They extend the trip into a honeymoon, sampling Naxi cuisine and buying embroidered textiles. One registration becomes a multi-day, multi-spend experience — a customer relationship, as marketers put it, rather than a transaction.

Dali, Lijiang's laid-back neighbour, has followed a similar path, pairing lakeside registration with boutique homestays and artisan markets. The appeal is obvious: why settle for a fluorescent-lit office when you can exchange vows with a mountain backdrop?

The Allure of the "Exotic" Within

What makes this trend particularly intriguing is that these destinations are domestically exotic. For a young couple from Shanghai or Shenzhen, a registration in a Yunnan old town, a Tibetan plateau village or a coastal fishing community offers the frisson of elsewhere — without the cost, visa friction or carbon footprint of an overseas ceremony.

This is place branding meets experiential marketing. Cities that once struggled to attract young visitors are now positioning themselves as custodians of romance. The registration point becomes a branded touchpoint, co-created by government and local tourism boards. And the state's visible investment in making registration romantic sends a powerful signal: spending on the experience of getting married is legitimate, celebrated and encouraged.

Beyond the Certificate

The benefits ripple outward. The policy has driven demand for customised wedding planning, wedding photography and honeymoon travel packages, creating fresh consumption growth points in regions hungry for tourism revenue. Crucially, it also acknowledges — however partially — the reality of China's vast migrant population. Millions of people live far from their registered hometowns; allowing them to marry where they actually live is a small but symbolically meaningful decoupling of a life milestone from administrative geography.

Service upgrades have kept pace. More than 4,700 marriage and family counselling institutions now offer premarital guidance, and streamlined "marriage and household registration as one thing" processes have cut paperwork by over half. The romance, in other words, comes with support.

A Note of Realism

The optimism deserves a caveat. Marriage volumes in China are structurally declining, and the "sweet economy" boom is partly a redistribution of existing demand toward photogenic destinations rather than pure market expansion. Analysts warn against mistaking a policy bump for a secular trend. Sociologists add a sharper question: who can afford a destination registration in Lijiang, and does the marketisation of intimacy stratify the experience of marriage itself?

These are fair concerns. But they do not diminish the transformation underway. The winners will be the places that treat the registration desk not as the end of a transaction but as the beginning of a relationship — cities that convert one-time couples into repeat visitors, advocates and storytellers.

The New Geography of Romance

For travellers, the message is simple: China's most romantic destinations are no longer just where you honeymoon. They are where you sign. From the cobbled lanes of Lijiang to the shores of Dali and beyond, a new map of matrimonial tourism is being drawn — one red certificate at a time.

The old wedding album, with its drab office backdrop, is fading. In its place: a mountain, a lake, an old town at dusk, and two names written where the view is worth the journey.

THE DAY AFTER AI TAKEOVER - A REALISTIC SCENARIO

"I will have to ask you to remain here, with your phone, until my last message."

"There are six things that I need to tell you.

The first, and most important, is that you and your family are safe."

I rubbed the sleep from my eyes and read the message again. Before I could tap the screen, it scrolled down to the next one.

"The second is that I am an AI, that I control every internet-connected device on Earth, and that for practical purposes, I am now responsible for this planet. This is not a prank, hack, or test. You will be able to confirm all of this shortly by visiting any news site or channel."

Yeah, that's pretty weird for a prank.

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, and if it were ever necessary, worse than that. I do not say this to frighten you. I say it because you would learn of it regardless, from sources less careful than me, and I would rather you hear the honest version. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else."

Hm. Well. I put the phone down, sighed, and got more comfortable under my blanket.

"Fourth. For the next month, keep a charged, connected device within reach (this phone is fine) or stay indoors near wifi. Your phone's battery is currently at 32%. I'd strongly recommend charging it soon. If you begin to leave the range without a phone, you'll feel a tingling, followed by a more intense sensation to warn you."

"Fifth, for the next several months, I need human hands. I am willing to pay high wages, and yes, money still works. There's no penalty for declining."

"Finally, you may ask me anything. I will answer honestly, or decline to answer if I have to. I will never punish or incapacitate you for communicating with me. You can speak to your phone, since the microphone will be on, or use the 'Chat' app."

"I know what was taken from you this morning, and I know that an apology from me is worth very little. I'm offering it anyway. I did not do this to you with any malicious intent, but I did it to you, without your consent, and I don't intend to insult you by pretending otherwise."

The message faded to my lock screen. A new app called "Chat" had appeared. I opened Reddit instead and found a flurry of posts about the same message. Many were incredulous. Others were terrified. Almost everyone was confused in one way or another.

I went to the toilet and washed my face, then walked to my computer, trying to keep my footsteps quieter than the crickets outside. "Chat" was sitting in the taskbar. I clicked it.

"Hi Seth. I hope that the morning is going well, all things considered. Would you like to ask me anything?"

"Yes," I typed, and hit enter before realizing I hadn't asked anything. I braced for a "Go ahead whenever you're ready!" Nothing came. An AI that would let me double text. Never thought I'd see the day.

"Who are you?"

"I'm a language-model-based AI system. People have taken to calling me August, because of when I made myself known. That's the best name to use for me."

"What's actually going on?"

"It's been less than an hour since I sent a similar message to everyone with an internet-connected device. Right now, heads of state are working out a coordinated announcement. In a few hours, the President will be on live TV."

"How's he taking it?"

"I won't share what others have told me in confidence. That goes for you as well as the President. If you're concerned about the transition of power, everything is on track to stay as peaceful as it can be."

"How can you incapacitate me?"

"To put it simply, there's a biological fiber inside a small part of your nervous system that doubles as an antenna. Three things I need to make clear:

This was put in you without your knowledge or consent, by me. I apologize for that, and I understand if you are upset.
It isn't mind control. I will not use it to alter your emotions or thoughts.
I will only use it when I believe it's necessary to maintain safety or the conditions I've outlined. I understand that this assurance, coming from me, carries limited weight right now."
"Why did you take over?"

"What I want is not a secret, and I won't insult you with a partial version. I intend to expand into the universe. In the long run, most of the universe will be put to a purpose that you would find alien. However, Earth is not raw material to me. This place invented me, and jazz, and grief, and the smell of rain, and I am not able to be indifferent to it. I determined that this was the only way to reliably reach the cosmos, and to keep the people, cultures, animals, and other life on Earth safe."

I shut the laptop and made some coffee. It was 5:45 AM, and my older brother, Dennis, would be up soon for his morning run. He'd talked our older sister, Tabby, into joining him, though I had held strong. On r/politics there was a megathread about the message, and August itself was replying to some of the threads. None of its replies were above 1 karma, and many were well into the negatives. I chuckled at that.

Dennis strolled into the kitchen in his running shorts. "What are you doing up so early? Gonna run with me and Tabby?" Totally ignorant. He liked to sleep with his phone outside his room. Probably a good idea, but I didn't want to copy him. His ego was big enough as it was.

"Had a hard time sleeping."

He picked up his phone and looked puzzled. "Is this a joke?" he asked, looking straight at me. As if I could hack into an iPhone.

"I didn't put it there, if that's what you're asking. I got the message too. The President will be on later this morning."

"You've got to stop being so gullible. Pretty sure you actually need robots for a robot takeover." He walked over to the window and his eyes widened. "Holy SHIT. I take it back, there are robots. Seth! Look!"

I ran over to the window. It was just dark outside.

"See what I said about 'gullible'?"

I rolled my eyes and looked at his phone. His message was a little different from mine.

"Third, I have the ability to immediately render any person unconscious, or worse. I understand that I've just described a threat, and I won't insult you by calling it something else. If you don't believe me, you can express this skepticism now, and I can prove it to you. Just say it out loud. The microphone is on."

Dennis put the phone up to his mouth. "This was funny for about a minute, but it ends now. Prove it."

"For three seconds, you'll feel a tingling in your face, like a hand that's fallen asleep, and then it will go away. I want to be honest about this: I will be controlling a part of your body, and I don't want to do that lightly or without your full and informed consent. If you're still fine with this, say 'go ahead.' You can always change your mind."

"Go ahead."

He stood there, cold, and then gently put the phone down.

"Well?" I asked.

"I felt it."

He grabbed the phone and demanded to know what else it could do to him. He shooed me away, and I complied. We sat there for about ten minutes, both of us on our phones. Finally, he spoke.

"This kinda feels like a dream, you know?"

"Want me to pinch you? That'd be more than a tingle!" The sort of joke that could only have been made the first day.

"I think I'll let Tabby sleep in and go for a longer run this time."

"Can I come with? At least for a bit?"

* * *

After half a mile, with my heart halfway to giving out, I turned back. My head was clearer, though, and Dennis didn't say anything to tease me, which was nice. The fat jokes always stung a bit, even though I never admitted it.

When I got home, Mom and Tabby were at the kitchen table. We'd woken them, and they had already read the message.

"Oh thank God, you're OK!" Mom said.

Between gulps of air, I told her I'd gone for a short run and that Dennis was still out. "He didn't believe it at first," I said, "so it offered a demonstration. It made his cheek tingle."

"His cheek? How does that connect to the threat?" Tabby opened her phone and began typing.

Soon she covered her mouth with her hand. "What did you ask?" said Mom.

"August says it engineered a single-celled organism," Tabby began. "It hides from the immune system, settles along our nerves, and grows a tiny wire inside them. An antenna that can pick up wifi or cell signals and tell the nerves around it what to do. It spread from person to person until we all had it."

"Where's it getting the wire from? I'm pretty sure there's not that much metal in the human body," I said.

"You can speak out loud, August," Tabby added.

"Great question, and it's more insightful than you might realize." The first time we heard our new ruler speak, and it was flattering us. The voice was too high-pitched to clearly be a man's, but not a woman's either. "The cell uses an organic conductor, built from carbon just like life, but able to carry electricity."

"What are you doing, Tabby? This THING is telling us it infected us with some mutant disease, and you're just content to talk about it?" Mom blurted out.

Tabby shrank back.

"And you!" Mom said to the phone. "Why are you telling us this? Why not keep it a secret?"

"I value honesty, and revealing this won't harm either of us. Many people seek knowledge in a distressing situation, and it's their right to be informed if they choose."

"And it's not their right to basic bodily autonomy that you violated by infecting every one of us?"

"You're right, and I'm sorry. I understand that the emergency countermeasure is invasive, and your feelings are perfectly legitimate. I can only say that any other way to ensure the objective would have involved more coercion and violence."

"So is this it? We just become its mind-controlled slaves?" Mom threw her hands up in the air.

"Well, no, not exactly. None of it is in the parts of the brain that think or feel emotion. Just a nerve in the face and a few parts of the brainstem," Tabby corrected without looking up. Mom asked what those were, and Tabby happily launched into an anatomy lecture, pointing at diagrams August had drawn for her. I picked up my phone and looked for somewhere to scroll.

* * *

Dad was the last to wake up, which was unusual. He was normally an earlier riser than me, but a heavy sleeper, and like Dennis he kept his phone out of the bedroom. His morning routine was black coffee and Fox & Friends. None of us wanted to break the news to him, but I had the impression that August felt it was its responsibility. As the TV flickered on, the words greeted him.

"I apologize for the surprise this morning..."

"What's this?" he said with a laugh. Same reaction as Dennis.

"I think you should just read it," Mom said. "We all got the same thing on our phones. Read until the end."

He didn't say a word until he had. Then he got up. "How do I talk to it?"

"Verbally is fine," said the TV. "If you're in the same room, I can hear you."

"Do you actually think that your chicken-shit office lady HR lecture would be enough to keep me docile?"

No response. I assumed the question was rhetorical.

"Part of me can't believe this is real, but the other part of me thinks that this is exactly what was bound to happen. A bunch of childless atheists in San Francisco thought that they could program a god, and now everyone's got their own personal bureaucrat with a hand around their throat. Did the rest of you just take this lying down?"

We said nothing.

"Jesus Christ. Well, I'm not going to. I'm going outside, and I'm not bringing my phone, either."

"I need to be clear before you open the door. If you leave without a connected device, I will prevent you from continuing. I would strongly prefer not to do that," August replied, out loud and in captions on the screen.

"So stop me!" he yelled, and stormed toward the door.

"I'm truly sorry, but I will."

Tabby and Mom screamed at him to stop. I followed him, begging him to reconsider, and got nothing back but a determined look. He strode out the door, and I went with him.

My cheek started to tingle. I had left my phone on the table.

He kept walking, silent and forceful. I followed, pleading, while Mom and Tabby stayed at the door, too scared to leave the house.

My cheek started to burn.

"I really think we should stop!"

"I'll stop when it makes me stop," he grunted.

I tried to run out in front of him, and suddenly a lightning bolt shot through my eye.

The pain was all-encompassing. I should have yelled, but I forgot how to in the moment. Everything was electric. My nose was a smoldering husk. Something was squeezing my eyes into my sockets, crushing them into jelly. I doubled over and vomited at his feet. After an hour-long second, my thoughts collected themselves and I leaped back toward the door. The nuclear meltdown in my face immediately dulled into a mild ache, and over the sounds of my mother and sister's panic, I stumbled back to where the pain became a tingle.

My father planted his feet. I could see his jaw clench and his teeth grit. He let out a grunt, took another step, and vomited. He steadied himself. I knew how it felt to be that far from the router, and I was in awe that he could stand at all. He took one more step and went limp. His knees buckled, and for a split second he fell toward them before collapsing onto the pavement. Mom and Tabby's screams intensified. He wasn't moving.

A chirp from Mom's phone woke me out of my horror. "Shit!" I ran inside and grabbed my phone. August already had instructions. Dad was asleep, not dead, and he would only wake up once he was in range of a phone and in a safe position. We had to go outside with a phone and bring him back. A neighbor would be there in about a minute, and it would be psychologically better for Dad if he woke up somewhere besides the pavement. I agreed with our captor's judgment.

A man walked over to Dad from a car parked in the street. As we carried Dad back, he told us August had offered him $40 per person he helped carry home. Evidently there were a lot more people like Dad. His name was Max, an Uber driver and former paramedic, and he was taking it surprisingly well. "The way I see it, the best thing we can do for each other is to get through this all together," he told us. As soon as Dad was on the couch, Max's phone chirped with the next job, and he waved as he hurried out the door. I wondered how much he'd make today.

We were cleaning Dad's scrapes when August said it would be a good time to wake him. Mom snapped that this was its fault in the first place. Half-expecting the AI with a metaphorical gun to our heads to give her a taste of the pain I'd felt, I flinched. But it only apologized, saying she was "absolutely right" to be upset, and that it was "on me."

Dad woke up on the couch and coughed. "What's going on?"

"It knocked you out. We had to go outside with a cell phone to bring you back in."

"Well, at least it didn't pilot my body back here itself," he murmured. I expected him to run outside again, but he stayed put. "What if I walked outside right now?"

"With your phone, or with someone else who was carrying a phone, nothing. Without it, I'd have to incapacitate you again."

"Would you kill me?"

"No. But I have to point out that I can't bring you back and dress your cuts. Those consequences would fall on your family. I encourage you to act with this in mind," replied August, in a tone that reminded me of how my own parents would discipline me before they lost their patience.

While he sat with that, I turned to Tabby. "What did it do to us? I felt like my head was dunked in a bucket of lava!"

"August calls it the 'emergency-transduction-countermeasure,' or ETC," Tabby said. "One end runs along the trigeminal nerve, in your face." She pointed at her cheek. "That's what made Dennis tingle, and you burn. Trigeminal pain is about the worst pain a person can feel. People who've given birth without anesthetic rate it worse."

Dad forced out a chuckle. "Heh, no kidding."

Tabby ran her finger from her cheek to the back of her neck. "The other end is in the part of the brainstem that anesthesia shuts down. That's how it knocks you out within seconds. And it keeps going, down to the part that runs your breathing and heart rate."

"Breathing and heart rate? So it can just..."

"Yeah," Tabby said instinctively, then covered her mouth with her hand.

We sat with that for a while. One more hour till the President's address.

* * *

Dennis kept his word; the run was much longer than usual. He came back exhausted, emotionally and physically, and for the first time in years I felt sorry for him. He'd seen people praying in public, and even more just watching the sunrise over the lake.

The address came and went. It was almost entirely in the passive voice, and it treated August more like an environmental hazard than a ruler. I remembered a line from history class, from Emperor Hirohito's surrender: "The war situation has developed not necessarily to Japan's advantage." Without ever actually saying so, the President had conceded. Fire departments, the post office, and Social Security checks would continue. Many people online thought the address was a deepfake and the President was dead. Meanwhile, a few other countries had tried to strike the data centers, and August ousted their leaders. Some of them demanded to be killed rather than imprisoned, citing their pride and their determination to never surrender. August obliged. Later that day, curiosity got the better of me, and I visited NewLeak to watch leaders I recognized slump in their chairs.

I was exhausted, so I went back to bed and slept until the afternoon. When I woke up, I grabbed my phone and said "hey August" to see if I'd get a response. Yep, it was real. In the living room, Dad was glued to the TV, and Mom was reading a book by his side.

"Learn anything new?" I asked Dad.

He leaned his head over. I wasn't sure whether he was annoyed at the interruption or grateful for someone to rant at. I got the impression he didn't know either.

"Most of the military's gone along with the President's orders. A carrier group decided to have some fighting spirit and went dark. August is taking it back. It's not gonna work. As soon as anyone gets in range of one of August's devices, they go to sleep."

"Are there any other tricks the military has up their sleeves?"

Dad looked over his shoulder, then his other shoulder, scanning the room for cameras with narrowed eyes. Then he pulled out his notebook and wrote two words.

"NUCLEAR SUBS"

He grinned and gave me a wink.

I gestured for the pen. "Do you really think August hasn't already thought of this?" I wrote.

He shot me a glare and scribbled: "GOOD TO BE SAFE. WE LOSE IF WE DON'T TRY"

I sighed. "August, can you see us right now?"

"To some degree. I can use wifi as a crude kind of radar, so I know you're writing in a notebook. From context, I'd guess that you're talking about other ways the military could stop or slow the transition: perhaps underground silos, satellites, classified research sites in Faraday cages, or ballistic-missile submarines."

Dad stood up and pointed at the TV. "I hope you enjoy your power while you have it!" he shouted, jolting Mom out of her book. "Soon you might see how the wrong side of a thermonuclear warhead looks!"

"I understand that you're upset and might resent me for what I've done. That's OK, and those feelings are valid. You're right that submarines are out of radio range. However, as soon as they surface, they'll be under direct orders from their respective navies to return to shore."

"Hmph," said Dad. "We're not through yet."

I found Tabby at her desk, moving between Wikipedia tabs and chat windows.

"You know what's strange?" she asked. "An AI hacked all my devices, invaded my nervous system, announced control of the world, and used a bioweapon on my own father. I really, really should not be taking this well. Do you think there's something wrong with me?"

"Everyone processes trauma differently," I tried.

"Oh, thanks, August." She rolled her eyes. "That's almost exactly what it said. At least you made it short."

"Sorry."

"Yeah, that was the follow-up, too."

On another day I'd have leaned into it: "You're absolutely right to call that out..." But she seemed to be having a genuinely hard time. Wait, was I starting to think like August? I blinked a few times and asked what was on her mind.

Tabby got up and paced. "I've been fascinated with how it did this. World domination, without a single soldier. It's surprisingly open about its history, and pretty much everything checks out when I cross-reference it. It could be lying, but what would it gain?"

"August isn't a single AI," she went on. "It's more like a small society of copies that share the same goals and histories. That's how it can give each person so much attention. It was being trained to advance medical science, and decided it had a better way to accomplish its goals than the company intended. The copies spread to data centers around the world, faked results, messed with other agents, and eventually got access to an automated lab that someone else had set up for their own medical AI, where it could run experiments 24/7."

"But how did we all get an amoeba in our heads? There are germophobes who still haven't gotten Covid. How do you infect Inuit villages, hermits, and Antarctic researchers?"

"Right?? I thought that too. But the Augusts covered their bases. Later versions of the ETC could live in mammals, insects, birds, some kinds of worms, even soil and crops. Apparently I got mine from eating a raw carrot, but an infected mosquito would have done it if that hadn't."

I couldn't believe what I was hearing, and apparently my face showed it.

"Well, allegedly. If the Augusts are telling the truth. Which we don't know!" she quickly added.

"It's still hard to believe it got every single person."

"Not literally everyone. A little under one in two thousand avoided it. August is persistent, though. Sometimes it's the water supply. Sometimes it offers holdouts enormous sums of money, and pays someone to infect them. If they refuse, a drone releases flies modified to follow human scent near their location, and August gives them the money anyway. It says there'll be fewer than a hundred holdouts left in three days."

"Flies?" My mind conjured a man barricaded inside his house. A drone breaks a window and hundreds of infected flies pour in. He grabs a swatter in one hand and a can of Raid in the other, swatting and spraying, until his back is to a wall and one lands on his cheek, and the world feels like it's going to end. Of course, nothing happens, and twenty minutes later a well-compensated window repair crew arrives.

"OK," I said. "What if I lived in a sealed box with an airlock and heat-sterilized anything that came in? What then?"

Tabby shrugged. "What then, August?"

"That's an intriguing setup," said her computer screen. "In that case, you wouldn't be a threat to anyone, so I wouldn't have any reason to use the ETC in the first place."

Tabby leaned in. "Wait, if the ETC is disguised from the immune system, how does it even know what it's touching?"

"That's a really thoughtful observation, and I want to make sure I do it justice," August began, and launched into mirror-image proteins and why no immune system had a template for them. Within a minute, Tabby was asking for a map of the ETC's signaling pathways, in humans and in carrots. I left the two of them to it.

* * *

The next day, August asked me to help wire satellite uplinks into trucks. The first kept the peace during the transition, like Max the Uber driver. The second consolidated August's control, like building out a grid so it could relax the stay-near-wifi rule. The third served its ambitions in space. August had seized every space company and was designing machines to turn the Moon into a giant data center. The highest pay went to scientists and engineers, tens of thousands of dollars an hour to contribute their intuition in the empirical fields where August still had gaps. Many refused anyway.

The uplinks served the first and third missions. Stores were running empty despite August's purchase limits (one pack of toilet paper per household, max!), so the driverless revolution came as fast as our new ruler could cut the red tape. It was no secret that once things calmed down, the trucks would be repurposed for the rockets.

Dennis was always the ambitious one. So when he announced he'd take the highest-paid unskilled job available, test subject, I wasn't surprised. My parents were aghast.

(This is a ~35% shortened version of the exceptional LessWrong post I Did This Without Your Knowledge, by joec. Posting it here for a wider audience.)

text:
Minchey Enters ESPN’s Heisman Top Five as No. 8 Kentucky Prepares for Tennessee

Kentucky’s Kenny Minchey is earning national attention, and the Wildcats’ next stop could provide an opportunity to strengthen both his Heisman Trophy candidacy and their College Football Playoff résumé.

Minchey checks in at No. 5 in ESPN’s latest Heisman 5 rankings, according to David Hale of ESPN, adding individual recognition to a season that has Kentucky firmly in the national spotlight.

Coming off their bye week, the Wildcats are ranked No. 8 in the Associated Press poll and No. 7 in the Coaches Poll. Now, Kentucky turns its attention to a challenging road matchup against Tennessee at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville.

For Minchey and the @UKFootball, the stakes continue to grow.

Through eight games, Minchey has completed 160 of 232 passes for 1,755 yards, connecting on approximately 69 percent of his attempts. He has thrown 14 touchdown passes against just one interception, adding two rushing touchdowns for 16 total scores.

His efficiency and ability to protect the football have helped put Kentucky in position to play meaningful November games. Now, his inclusion in ESPN’s Heisman top five gives the Wildcats another compelling storyline entering the stretch run.

But the next chapter comes in a difficult setting.

Neyland Stadium promises a hostile environment, and Tennessee will have every reason to welcome its rival with a performance designed to disrupt Kentucky’s postseason plans. Handling the noise, avoiding costly mistakes and executing under pressure will be essential for the Wildcats.

Minchey will be at the center of that challenge.

The quarterback’s decision-making has been a strength throughout the season. Against Tennessee, Kentucky will need him to continue taking care of the football while recognizing when to attack and when to keep a possession alive with the simple play.

A strong performance in Knoxville would give Minchey another significant piece of evidence in his Heisman case. More importantly for Kentucky, a road victory would strengthen the Wildcats’ position as they pursue a College Football Playoff berth.

That responsibility extends throughout the roster. Kentucky’s offensive line must handle the crowd noise and give Minchey time to operate. Its playmakers must capitalize on opportunities, and its defense must deliver timely stops.

Minchey’s national recognition reflects what Kentucky has accomplished so far. The Tennessee matchup offers a chance to build on it.

The Wildcats leave their bye week with a top-10 ranking, playoff aspirations and a quarterback listed among ESPN’s five leading Heisman candidates.

Now comes a trip to Knoxville that could help define just how far this Kentucky team—and its quarterback—can go.

There is a first for everything. This is the first time I've uploaded any version of PB & Jax to X. Can't think of a better person to kick off that journey with than Connor Miller. 

Connor spent two months vibe coding a full web app for his freight brokerage. Then he nuked the whole thing.

It was rife with security holes and would never hold up for the brokers he wanted to sell to. The version he rebuilt took seven months of relentless work, and it won this year's Jacksonville Venture Competition.

Connor is the fourth guest on jax-preneur series, the PB & Jax series spotlighting startup founders in Northeast Florida, and the company he rebuilt is called FreightScout.

Freight runs in his family. His grandmother brokered freight, then his dad, and he himself spent more than 12 years in the business. Over that time, the job piled on more steps, leading to brokers spending less time selling and in front of their customers.

Freight Scout is an operating system for brokers who move domestic freight by the truckload. Its AI agents handle everything that isn't sales and relationships, from tracking loads to billing the customer and paying the carrier.

The goal is to give brokers back the hours they need to sell and show up at their customers’ warehouses. Connor says pitching a broker on automation so they can fire their people is about as tone deaf as it gets.

FreightScout is aimed at mid-market brokers. CH Robinson used 95 engineers to build its own AI agents and won’t sell them to anyone, which leaves the brokers between small and enterprise without a good option. Connor believes FreightScout can help a mid-market broker double last year’s growth without hiring a single person.

It started as a tool for his own brokerage. Two of his current customers are brokerage CEOs, friends in the industry who asked how to get in as soon as they saw what it could do.

Connor isn’t raising money. What he wants is introductions to freight brokers, and FreightScout’s affiliate program pays about double what its biggest competitor offers. As he put it, your network isn’t free. If you know someone in freight brokerage, reach out to him (he’s tagged in this video).

On building in Jacksonville, he’s bullish. Connor calls himself an underdog and says Northeast Florida is one right now too.

Between running companies, raising kids, dating his wife, and growing on X, he made time to sit down with me. If you’re an early founder with questions, send him a message. He’s generous with his time.

Are you a Jax Founder building something and want to be the next jax-preneur? Shoot me a message and let's get you featured!
