text:
AGENDA 2027: AFTER THE BALLOT

The Choices That Will Shape Kenya After Elections

Sifuna’s American Tour: The Diaspora Deserves More Than Another Fundraising Dinner

As Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna prepares for his anticipated tour of the United States, I hope he will depart from the familiar script of Kenyan politicians visiting the diaspora.

Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i have both attracted considerable interest among Kenyans in America. I will resist the temptation to discuss the ethnic composition of their audiences. I am not among those Kenyans who pretend ethnicity has no role in political mobilisation, whether in Kenya or elsewhere. Charity begins at home. Period.

But a politician with national ambitions must eventually transcend the comfort of his ethnic constituency. Sifuna’s tour is an opportunity to do so.

Kenya has an estimated four million citizens living abroad. According to the Central Bank of Kenya, formal remittances reached approximately Sh650 billion in 2025. A broader household survey by the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics estimated Sh931.8 billion in cash and in-kind remittances over the 12 months ending May 2025.

That is an extraordinary amount of money. It is also an extraordinary demonstration of patriotism, expressed in exhausting shifts, missed holidays and transfers made at considerable personal sacrifice.

Our people are among our most valuable exports, although the uncomfortable discussion about the kinds of labour we export can wait for another day. The relationship between Kenya and its diaspora remains disproportionately extractive. We celebrate the money. We rarely celebrate the people.

Where is the love?

To its credit, the Kenya Kwanza administration has strengthened the institutional recognition of the diaspora, including through the State Department for Diaspora Affairs. These are useful beginnings. But a considerable distance remains between recognising the diaspora in government documents and making Kenyans abroad feel genuinely valued.

Many Kenyans overseas work heartbreaking shifts in unglamorous jobs. Others are professionals in prestigious institutions. Some left to pursue opportunity; others left because the economy offered them little choice. What unites many of them is a continuing emotional investment in Kenya. They want their children to know where they came from, their parents to live decently, and the country they left behind to become somewhere they can return to with pride.

Unfortunately, relations between Kenyans at home and those abroad are not particularly healthy. Mutual suspicion runs high, sometimes disguised as humour and sometimes expressed with remarkable contempt. Those abroad are dismissed as arrogant people who have forgotten the realities of home. Those at home are accused of dependency, entitlement, and a troubling inability to understand that dollars do not grow on trees in America.

Somewhere between these two groups sits the terrible institution we call black tax.

The economy has made matters worse. Healthcare, education, rent and unemployment consume incomes before people can plan their futures, and those pressures inevitably travel across borders. I suspect that some of the growth in remittances reflects the growing demands placed on senders, in addition to the growing number of Kenyans abroad. That hypothesis deserves investigation before we celebrate every increase as evidence of national prosperity.

Black tax cannot become Kenya’s permanent substitute for functioning public services. A Kenyan working overseas should not be automatically appointed the emergency treasury secretary of an entire extended family.

This brings me to Sifuna. His presidential ambitions present an opportunity to put a serious question on the national agenda: What would a humane, mutually beneficial relationship between Kenya and its diaspora actually look like?

First, his engagement should be genuinely national. Sifuna belongs to Kenyans as much as he belongs to the Bukusu community. The conversation should include Kenyans from every region, ethnicity, profession and economic background.

Second, the tour should not become another fundraising exhibition. Campaigns require resources, and there is nothing objectionable about citizens voluntarily financing politicians whose ideas they support. But the diaspora deserves something more substantial than an expensive dinner, a photograph with a politician and a speech promising to rescue Kenya. Let fundraising be transparent, voluntary and properly accounted for. Let policy dominate the conversation.

Third, Kenyans abroad need credible protection for their investments. Too many have sent money home for land, houses or businesses, only to discover that the property, contractor, relative or opportunity was not quite what had been represented. Fraud is hardly unique to the diaspora, but distance makes victims particularly vulnerable. Kenya needs accessible property verification, transparent land transactions, reliable dispute resolution and stronger enforcement. A Kenyan in Washington, London, Doha or Melbourne should be able to conduct legitimate business without relying on a chain of intermediaries. These reforms should benefit every Kenyan, without establishing a privileged class of citizens abroad.

Fourth, we must think beyond remittances. Imagine diaspora money moving confidently into manufacturing, agriculture, technology, healthcare, infrastructure and growing businesses. Too much of it still ends up in another apartment block, another speculative plot or another family emergency.

Other countries offer useful lessons. Ireland has developed extensive networks connecting its diaspora to business, culture, public policy and national development, and its 2026-2030 diaspora strategy was informed by consultations with Irish communities abroad. Israel has long mobilised diaspora capital through development bonds. India has used diaspora bonds at critical moments, while its overseas professional networks have connected Indian businesses to international markets. None offers a magical formula, but all demonstrate that a diaspora can contribute far beyond household consumption.

Kenya already has a diaspora investment strategy. The task is to turn it into institutions people trust, with transparent projects, reasonable returns, credible safeguards and measurable results. I would love to see Kenya substantially increase the economic value of its diaspora relationships over the coming decade, perhaps even double it. That ambition must go beyond extracting twice as much money from people already supporting too many dependants. It should attract productive investment, create employment at home and eventually reduce the burden on those abroad.

Fifth, Kenya must take knowledge transfer seriously. Kenyans work in leading universities, hospitals, financial institutions, technology companies and research centres around the world, and some possess precisely the expertise Kenya needs. Yet our public appointments too often appear designed around political loyalty. Loyalists have a place in politics, but serious economic and technical decisions require serious people. Diaspora professionals should be able to advise ministries, mentor local institutions, undertake temporary assignments and collaborate with Kenyan businesses without abandoning successful careers overseas or submitting to political patronage.

Sixth, consular welfare deserves greater attention. Kenyans facing exploitation, detention, workplace abuse, bereavement or other emergencies abroad should know where to seek help and what assistance to expect. Our embassies and consulates perform important work, sometimes under difficult circumstances, but service standards, emergency response and accountability can improve. Better data would also help government understand who its citizens abroad are, where they live, what they need and what they can contribute.

Finally, the relationship must become genuinely two-way. Diaspora engagement should not mean politicians arriving with ready-made speeches, collecting applause and contributions, then disappearing until the next election. For Sifuna, a better approach could begin with a published diaspora policy blueprint, open consultations and a clear mechanism for continuing engagement after the tour. It would also mean answering difficult questions: What can realistically be achieved? What would require legislation? What would it cost? Which reforms could begin immediately, and which would take years?

The diaspora does not need another politician promising heaven. It needs a government that understands why so many Kenyans had to leave home, respects what they have built elsewhere and creates conditions in which their patriotism can find meaningful expression.

That is the standard against which Sifuna’s American engagement, and those of every politician seeking national leadership, should be judged. Let him listen more than he speaks. Let him offer a workable, believable and ambitious blueprint.

Above all, let us stop treating Kenyans abroad as walking dollar/euro/dinar/pound/yen/rand signs. They are citizens, partners and stakeholders in the country’s future.

Patriotism should not be a one-way money transfer.

The Ottoman Empire laid siege to Vienna twice, but neither siege occurred in what we normally call the Middle Ages:
1529 — First Siege of Vienna: Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent besieged Vienna from September 27 to October 15, 1529. This was during the early modern period, not the Middle Ages.
1683 — Second Siege of Vienna: An enormous Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged Vienna from July 14 to September 12, 1683. The siege was broken by a relief army led by the Polish king Jan III Sobieski.
If you're thinking of the famous 1683 siege, it was a pivotal event in European history. The Ottoman defeat marked a major turning point: thereafter, the Ottoman Empire increasingly lost ground in Central Europe to the Habsburgs.
The Middle Ages conventionally ended around 1450–1500, so the 1529 siege was only a few decades after the medieval period, while 1683 was well into the early modern era.

WALL STREET’S BIG WEEK: $AAPL, $PLTR, $AMD, U.S. MIDTERMS & THE JOBS REPORT

November 2–6, 2026 | U.S. Market Outlook

AI earnings. U.S. midterm elections. The October jobs report. Three major catalysts are converging in one trading week.

But the biggest opportunity may not come from predicting the headlines. It may come from understanding where market expectations have become too demanding.

$PLTR enters earnings after reporting 93% revenue growth last quarter. $AMD has guided for approximately $13B in quarterly revenue. Both face a market increasingly focused on whether extraordinary AI growth can translate into sustainable profits.

Meanwhile, Friday’s employment report could reshape interest-rate expectations and the valuations investors are willing to pay for that growth.

Here’s the calendar—and what I believe investors should actually be watching.

MONDAY, NOVEMBER 2 | AI SOFTWARE & APPLE

Economic Data (EST)

09:45 — S&P Global Manufacturing PMI (October)

10:00 — ISM Manufacturing PMI (October)

Earnings (After Market Close)

$AAPL — Apple

$PLTR — Palantir Technologies

Palantir may be one of the week’s most revealing AI earnings reports.

In Q2, Palantir delivered 93% year-over-year revenue growth, including 149% growth in U.S. commercial revenue. Its Q3 guidance calls for approximately $2.16B in revenue, implying roughly 83% annual growth, and approximately $1.29B in adjusted operating income.

Those are extraordinary numbers. But they also establish an extraordinary performance benchmark.

An earnings beat alone may not be enough if investors are already pricing in another substantial guidance increase. I will be watching U.S. commercial growth, large contract conversion, adjusted operating margins and whether management raises its full-year outlook.

For Apple, the more important question is whether iPhone demand, services growth and holiday-quarter guidance can support earnings expectations. Strong historical results matter less if forward guidance suggests slower demand or margin pressure.

TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 3 | MIDTERM ELECTIONS & THE AI HARDWARE TEST

Economic Data

10:00 — JOLTS Job Openings (September)

10:00 — Factory Orders (September)

Earnings (Before Market Open)

$SHOP — Shopify

$PFE — Pfizer

Earnings (After Market Close)

$AMD — Advanced Micro Devices

$ANET — Arista Networks

$BKNG — Booking Holdings

$AMGN — Amgen

AMD and Arista offer two complementary views of AI infrastructure spending.

AMD’s latest guidance calls for approximately $13B in Q3 revenue, representing around 41% year-over-year growth, with a non-GAAP gross margin of roughly 56%.

For AMD, I care about more than GPU demand. The real test is whether revenue growth comes with durable gross margins, competitive pricing and stronger future guidance.

Arista provides a different perspective: AI networking demand. If GPU spending remains strong but networking orders or customer deployments slow, that divergence could reveal where infrastructure expansion is becoming less synchronized.

Tuesday also brings the U.S. midterm elections. Early polls begin closing around 6 p.m. EST, with results arriving in stages throughout the evening and potentially beyond.

Investors should monitor changes in expectations for fiscal policy, regulation and government spending, but election-night volatility should not automatically be confused with a durable change in corporate earnings. There is no guaranteed time when control of Congress will be fully established.

WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 4 | EMPLOYMENT, SERVICES & THE NEXT AI LAYER

Economic Data

08:15 — ADP Private Employment (October)

10:00 — ISM Services PMI (October)

Earnings (Before Market Open)

$UBER — Uber

$MCD — McDonald’s

$NVO — Novo Nordisk

Earnings (After Market Close)

$QCOM — Qualcomm

$ARM — Arm Holdings

$APP — AppLovin

Wednesday’s earnings will help investors examine AI commercialization beyond data centers.

Qualcomm and Arm offer insight into handset demand, chip architecture and edge AI adoption. AppLovin provides a perspective on advertising technology and monetization, where improvements should ultimately be reflected in revenue quality and operating profitability.

Outside technology, Uber and McDonald’s can help reveal differences in consumer spending and price sensitivity, while Novo Nordisk will be closely watched for pharmaceutical demand and competitive developments.

The broader question is whether economic activity is supporting corporate margins—or whether companies are increasingly relying on pricing and cost reductions to protect earnings.

THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 5 | LABOR MARKET & SOFTWARE DEMAND

Economic Data

08:30 — Initial Jobless Claims

08:30 — Q3 Nonfarm Productivity & Unit Labor Costs (Preliminary)

Earnings (After Market Close)

$ABNB — Airbnb

$NET — Cloudflare

Cloudflare’s results will offer another test of enterprise technology spending. I will focus on the sustainability of growth, customer expansion, margins and whether increased AI-related demand is translating into stronger recurring revenue.

Airbnb provides another consumer-demand signal, particularly through bookings, average daily rates and forward travel expectations.

Weekly jobless claims and productivity data also matter. Rising productivity can help companies protect margins without relying entirely on price increases, while deteriorating labor conditions could threaten revenue growth.

FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 6 | THE WEEK’S BIGGEST MACRO CATALYST

08:30 — October Nonfarm Payrolls (NFP)

Including:

Nonfarm Payroll Growth

Unemployment Rate

Average Hourly Earnings (MoM & YoY)

10:00 — University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment (November Preliminary)

10:00 — Consumer Inflation Expectations (Preliminary)

Earnings (Before Market Open)

$MRNA — Moderna

Friday’s jobs report could influence the valuation framework for the entire equity market.

A softer labor market may reduce pressure on interest rates, potentially supporting long-duration growth stocks. But if hiring weakens too sharply, falling yields may not compensate for deteriorating earnings expectations.

Stronger employment could support the economic outlook while simultaneously keeping borrowing costs elevated.

The distinction matters: lower rates are not automatically bullish if the reason for those lower rates is a weakening economy.

I’ll be watching payroll revisions, unemployment, wage growth and Treasury yields together, rather than treating the headline payroll number as a standalone trading signal.

MY INVESTMENT PLAYBOOK FOR THE WEEK

My priority is to distinguish genuine improvements in business fundamentals from earnings results that merely satisfy expectations.

For $PLTR, the key is whether commercial growth and forward guidance justify the valuation investors are paying.

For $AMD and $ANET, I want evidence that AI infrastructure demand is translating into sustainable revenue growth without excessive margin pressure.

For the broader market, Friday’s employment report will help determine whether the macroeconomic environment continues to support elevated equity valuations.

I wouldn’t chase an earnings stock simply because it beats EPS estimates. I’d compare the new guidance against consensus, assess how much future growth is already priced in and look for a favorable risk/reward entry after the market has processed the results.

A sharp selloff could create an opportunity if the underlying earnings thesis remains intact. A rally could still be unattractive if valuations require unrealistic future performance.

The best investment setups emerge when market expectations and business fundamentals diverge—not simply when a stock moves sharply.

No FOMC rate decision is scheduled this week. The next major inflation catalyst is the October CPI report on November 10.

Which are you watching most closely this week: $PLTR, $AMD, $AAPL, or Friday’s jobs report?

All times U.S. Eastern Standard Time (EST). BMO = Before Market Open. AMC = After Market Close. Earnings schedules may change. Research commentary, not personalized investment advice.

A silver dragonfly hovered above the pond, its wings reflecting the afternoon sunlight. Beneath the surface, a turtle watched the performance with the expression of someone who had attended the same concert every summer for fifty years.

The mathematician wrote an equation on the kitchen window using a bar of soap. By morning, condensation had blurred the symbols into something resembling a mountain range, and she decided the result was more beautiful than her original calculation.

A traveling circus arrived in a village where nobody remembered purchasing tickets. The performers erected their tents anyway, and by sunset the mayor was juggling oranges while the schoolteacher attempted to tame an unusually opinionated goose.

The old woman kept seven clocks in her living room, each showing a different time. When visitors asked which one was correct, she smiled and said that every clock was right somewhere, although none of them had ever helped her catch a train.

A submarine passed beneath a drifting iceberg whose blue interior glowed like an illuminated cathedral. The captain slowed the vessel, allowing the crew a few silent moments before the darkness swallowed the enormous frozen sculpture.

The gardener discovered a sunflower growing through the cracked pavement behind the grocery store. Rather than remove it, the shopkeeper painted a small yellow arrow on the wall and labeled the unlikely flower the neighborhood's official botanical monument.

A philosopher ordered coffee in a railway station and began arguing with the vending machine about free will. The machine accepted his coins, dispensed hot chocolate instead, and offered no explanation for its apparent philosophical position.

The village blacksmith fashioned a tiny iron crown for a stray cat that visited his workshop each morning. The cat refused to wear it, preferring to sleep on the king's unfinished horseshoes, where the sunlight was considerably warmer.

At the edge of a distant desert, an astronomer watched the first stars emerge above the dunes. She had spent her career calculating the distances between galaxies, yet tonight she was content simply to sit beside a small fire and wonder what tomorrow might bring.

text:
In a nationwide televised address on October 31, 2026, Tusk accused Russia of supporting the Polish opposition through an "army of online trolls" and "pro-Russian forces globally," linking this directly to the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal. However, multiple sources—including Russian media and reports from the Chinese-language outlet *https://t.co/H8ZB1UqY24*—have explicitly noted that Tusk failed to provide any concrete evidence to substantiate these claims. The Russian side, represented by Dmitry Medvedev, responded with sarcasm, while the camp of the Polish president labeled Tusk a "pathological liar."

**Context and Timing of Tusk’s Address**

Tusk’s nationwide address followed a sharp escalation in the Constitutional Tribunal crisis. On October 30, Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced the one-month suspension of the Tribunal’s president, Bogdan Szewinczkowski, and his deputy, effectively assuming control of the institution herself. President Nawrocki cut short an overseas trip to return urgently to Warsaw, describing the move as a "coup d'état." Police surrounded the Tribunal building, leading to a standoff with protesters.

In his address, Tusk characterized the conflict as a case of external interference. He claimed that the opposition was "supported globally by pro-Russian forces," had "deployed an army of Russian online trolls" in the conflict, and had even "received public praise from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue." Yet, he offered no details regarding which specific accounts were involved, who operated them, or what direct links they might have to the Kremlin.

**Confirmation of a "Lack of Evidence"**

Multiple sources have independently confirmed that Tusk presented no evidence. The Russian newspaper *Rossiyskaya Gazeta* explicitly stated, "Tusk, of course, did not provide any evidence." A report by https://t.co/H8ZB1UqY24 (republished by NetEase) also noted: "However, RT pointed out that Tusk provided no evidence to support these allegations, nor did he offer any further details regarding the specific online accounts in question or those backing them." A commentary in the Russian publication *Argumenty i Fakty* was even sharper: "No evidence is needed—rabid Western Russophobes will swallow it all, and then ask for more."

Russia’s reaction: Sarcasm and denial

Medvedev responded on X with heavy sarcasm: "I love this mantra! A US election? It’s the Russians (who interfered). Migrants in Spain? That’s the Russians’ (fault)! A constitutional coup in Poland? Must be the Russians! Thanks! Nothing unites us quite like our own immense power!" He had previously characterized the events in Poland as a "coup," comparing Tusk’s camp to "Ukrainian Nazis who stripped the Constitutional Court of its authority."

An important distinction: The cryptocurrency allegations in April vs. the "troll farm" allegations in October

The document mentions that, "a month earlier," Tusk had accused the opposition of receiving funding from Russian criminal organizations via the platform Zondacrypto. This allegation, made in April 2026, is separate from the "online troll" accusations that surfaced in October. The April claim was more specific: Tusk alleged in parliament that the funds flowing through Zondacrypto were linked to the "Bratva" (Russian organized crime) and Russian intelligence services. He claimed the company had sponsored politicians from the Law and Justice (PiS) party and the far-right Confederation party, as well as the CPAC conference held in Rzeszów in March 2025—an event that took place five days before the presidential election and was attended by Nawrocki. This allegation was reportedly based on information from Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW). While Zondacrypto did not respond to inquiries from the AP, the company stated that it is cooperating with an investigation by Polish authorities.

The "troll farm" allegations from October, by contrast, lack such a specific source of information. It reframes a domestic struggle for judicial power as foreign interference, yet provides no verifiable details.

The Essence of the Constitutional Court Crisis: A Domestic Power Struggle

Reports from TVP Info clarify the root of the crisis: on March 13, 2026, parliament elected six new judges to the Constitutional Court, but President Nawrocki invited only two to be sworn in, rejecting the other four. On April 9, those four took the oath of office on their own, within the parliamentary premises. This dispute—centered on "who is entitled to serve as a judge and make decisions regarding the Court’s operations"—has effectively paralyzed the institution since 2023. Tusk’s government has sought to reform the judicial system, while the Constitutional Court—aligned with the Law and Justice (PiS) party—has resisted.

Verdict

Tusk’s allegations regarding a "Russian troll farm" were leveled at the height of a domestic political crisis, serving to transform a struggle for control over the judiciary into a national security issue. The verifiable facts are as follows: he made the accusations without providing public evidence; Russia denied them with a sarcastic retort; and the President’s camp dismissed them as "lies." Whether Russia is, in fact, coordinating online support for the opposition in Poland cannot be confirmed or refuted based on currently available public information. While Tusk’s April allegations concerning Zondacrypto were supported by information from the Internal Security Agency (ABW), his October claims about a "troll farm" lack a similar level of substantiation.

text:
Epilogue, What Remains After Halloween (Halloween Monster Roleplay 6) End

Halloween passes.

The bells of St. Brigid's Ossuary ring one last time as the night comes to an end, but they no longer announce changes to the past. Their sound travels through the halls, down the staircases, and into the forgotten chambers beneath the sanctuary, where the Skeleton Army and Rosarah held the ancient threat at bay while I made my final decision.

The bells are finally allowed to be bells again. I could have erased this place. I could have wiped away every memory of the Ossuary, every tragedy, every mistake, every prisoner who had ever walked its halls. I could have made it so none of this had ever happened, so that Blake never died, Rosarah never suffered, and the Father never built his sanctuary.

For one brief moment, I wanted to. But this place was real. The pain was real. And Blake's sacrifice was real. To erase it all would have been another kind of cruelty, another attempt to convince the world that suffering could be solved by pretending it never happened. That was what the Father would have done.

So I made a different choice. I took away the Ossuary's power to change history. The bells can no longer rewrite lives, erase names, or bend the past to fit somebody else's idea of perfection. The old records have stopped changing. The corridors no longer rearrange themselves to accommodate forgotten events, and the dead are finally allowed to remain dead without the world trying to make them something else.

The past belongs to the past.

And the future, for better or worse, belongs to those who live in it.

The Father remains.

Weakened, diminished, and stripped of much of the power that made him so terrifying, he still lingers within the sanctuary, a shadow of the being he once was. He can no longer force completion upon others, nor can he remake a person's history simply because he believes he knows what is best.

He has become something he never expected to be. A guide.

Under Sister Calva's watch, he now helps those who arrive at the Ossuary lost, frightened, or unable to understand what they have become. The two of them work together, although I doubt either would admit to enjoying the company. They listen, offer advice, and sometimes simply sit beside those who need somebody to stay.

No grand rituals. No promises of perfection. Just one act at a time.

Calva has changed, too, though not in the ways she once imagined. She still wears her habit and carries her billhook, but she no longer uses fear as her first answer. Her Hallow Knights remain near her, though their weapons are no longer raised against every inmate who dares to question her.

She has not been forgiven by everyone.

Rosarah, especially, has made it clear that forgiveness isn't something Calva can demand, earn through a single apology, or receive as payment for finally admitting she was wrong. And Calva has learned to live with that.

Sometimes she visits the garden and stands before Blake's statue. Other times, she sits near the sanctuary doors and listens to the bells. I think she is trying to understand how to live without the certainty that once kept her going.

For somebody who spent so long deciding the fates of others, learning to live with her own mistakes might be the hardest punishment of all.

Rosarah is still here. She isn't particularly pleased with her new body, which is understandable, considering that her new body is a nearly nine-foot iron nightmare with chains, claws, and a furnace in its chest.

The Iron Maiden.

She now patrols the Ossuary's halls, keeping the sanctuary safe from whatever horrors might still wander through its forgotten passages. Her blue flames burn quietly, and sometimes, late at night, I can hear her chains dragging across the stone. She talks to the remnants of Brother Mozgus that remain within the machine.

The voice isn't quite the man she remembers. It isn't enough to bring him back, and it never will be. But sometimes, when the halls are quiet, she hears something familiar in the way he speaks.

She still doesn't forgive Calva. But occasionally, she talks to her. Not because everything is fine. Not because the past has been repaired. But because Rosarah has finally been given the choice to speak, and this time, nobody is locking the door.

I think that matters more than either of them would admit.

The Skeleton Army has returned to its ancient duty. After the battle, Peter led the soldiers back beneath the Ossuary, where they restored their positions around the broken seal. It took time, patience, and more than a few arguments with the soldiers who insisted that standing perfectly still was a miserable way to spend eternity.

The seal holds. For now. Their memories of Queen Yvaine remain fragmented, and some of the soldiers still hesitate whenever they hear her name. I don't know whether she will ever return, or whether the army will ever fully understand what it was created to guard.

But they remember enough.

They remember that their duty existed long before me. And now, they have the freedom to question their commands.

They still guard the Ossuary, proudly standing throughout the grounds, but they are no longer treated as disposable weapons. They are given care, respect, and, when possible, a little time away from their posts.

Peter still visits the sanctuary gates. Sometimes he looks toward the tunnels. Sometimes he looks toward the sky. I wonder if he is waiting for his queen. Perhaps he always will be.

Bill and Bob are no longer sewn together. I may have had a hand in that. Their curse hasn't entirely disappeared, but they have learned to understand it, and with a little patience, they can now move independently for short periods. They still argue constantly, naturally, and I suspect their newfound freedom has only given them more opportunities to annoy one another.

Toll has finally stopped counting the bells. For the first time in what feels like forever, his mind is quiet. The Father helped him, though not through any grand act of magic. The work was slow, careful, and sometimes painful, but Toll is no longer trapped in the endless cycle of sounds that once drove him mad.

Now he keeps track of those who enter and leave the sanctuary. He has become something of a gatekeeper. He likes the work. He says there is comfort in knowing that when someone leaves, they have actually left.

As for the more dangerous inmates, they remain under careful watch. The Ossuary is still a strange and occasionally unpleasant place, after all, and not every monster can be trusted simply because the rules have changed.

The Bone Lady… I mean Femur Finder now helps direct the Skeleton Army, gathering scattered bones, tending to damaged soldiers, and making sure nobody gets left behind in the dark. It is peaceful work, and she seems genuinely happy with it.

She has all the children she could ever want.

Much to their dismay.

The invisible cat still follows her around, naturally, and occasionally knocks things off shelves that nobody can see, chased by Femer Finber’s invisible friend. Some things never change.

And Blake...

Well.

Blake is gone.

His remains were gathered with care, and a bronze statue was eventually raised in the garden near the Ossuary's gate. It shows him standing with his sleeves rolled up, one hand resting on his hip, looking like a man who has just finished a long day's work and is about to complain about somebody else's mess.

The plaque reads:

BLAKE BURTON

HEART OF THE OSSUARY

A GOOD FATHER

People stop there sometimes. Some leave flowers. Some leave little gifts. A few leave candy, which I think he would have appreciated.

They tell stories about him, even the ones who barely knew him. The man who helped keep the sanctuary running. The man who could fix almost anything with a little wax and a lot of complaining. The man who made a terrible choice, regretted it, and then made another choice when it mattered. He wanted to see his daughter again. He wanted to apologize. I never got to tell him whether I thought he would have been forgiven.

I don't know.

But I remember the sound of his voice. I remember the way he tried to smile. And I remember what he chose. Sometimes, when I visit the statue, I think about that little piece of wax that survived the ritual. I left it beneath the plaque, where it sits beside a small piece of ribbon from his old coat.

I don't know if his daughter will ever find her way to the Ossuary. I hope she does. And if she ever asks what happened to her father, I will tell her the truth. Not that he was perfect. Not that he was a hero all his life. But that, in the end, he was brave.

As for me...

I chose my own fate for a change.

The Ossuary no longer needs me, and I have no intention of becoming its new Father, Warden, or eternal king. So I used what remained of my power to give myself a body and send myself home. A real body. Warm skin. A heartbeat. Hands that occasionally get cold for absolutely no good reason.

It's weird.

I can choose my form more freely now, although that doesn't mean I have mastered it. I have already had a few embarrassing incidents involving misplaced fingers and one very unfortunate morning when my shadow decided it wanted to be a skeleton.

The Spirit of Halloween is still with me. Naturally. He has opinions about everything.

He insists that I am still an inferior version of him, which is a bold statement coming from someone who once panicked because he thought a particularly large moth was a demon. We have reached something of an understanding. He doesn't get to decide who I am. And I don't get to pretend he doesn't matter.

We are stuck with each other. Perhaps that isn't such a bad thing.

I still don't know everything about my past. Some names remain lost. Some memories are gone forever. There are things buried beneath the Ossuary that I have no intention of digging up, and questions about the Father, the Hole, and whatever waits beyond that ancient seal that I may never answer. But I have learned something.

Being whole doesn't mean being perfect. It doesn't mean having every memory restored, every wound healed, or every mistake erased. Sometimes, being whole simply means accepting that the pieces you have are yours. And that you are still allowed to grow. I think about the people I left behind. Rosarah, learning how to be heard. Calva, learning how to listen. The soldiers, learning how to choose. Toll, finally enjoying the silence. Blake, resting beneath the garden. And I wonder what they will become.

I suppose that's the point. Their stories belong to them now.

So, enjoy the people you care about while you have them. Learn to grow without demanding that you become somebody else. Accept who you are, and remember that your choices affect the people around you.

And if you ever find yourself wandering through a dark hallway, hearing bells where no bells should be ringing...

Well. Maybe don't follow them.

Or do.

I'm not your Warden.

Just remember to keep a healthy dose of the Spirit of Halloween.

Trust me. You're going to need it.

The End

text:
Lost in thought, per usual. Tonight’s agenda: purpose.

I don’t think I’m alone in this. I think many people contemplate their purpose or their reason for enduring the journey. There’s a lot of bullshit along the way, ya know. Regardless of circumstances, sometimes it’s just added salt to the wound.

I’ve thought a lot about life and how far I’ve come. Most of the time, I feel stuck. It’s a weird place to be. Like, I’m alive, right? Living in a first-world country, a geopolitical mogul in a game of Risk…even if it’s not to my liking. Yet I’m still weighed down by my own history. The pain that is me. The upbringing that belongs to me. A dark corridor full of doors you wouldn’t want to open.

I know one shouldn’t compare pain or lives lived. Yet a part of me buries my shit because when you look around, it really ain’t shit compared to what could’ve been. Especially when you consider environments and illness. It’s not fair tho, is it? To put the world against yourself.

Pain isn’t measured from person to person. We all experience the world separately, and we don’t get to choose what happens to us or the next person. What sense does it make to put ourselves in the struggle Olympics? We can only know our pain through our own experience. Doesn’t mean it’s lesser or greater than someone else’s. It’s just ours.

I struggle with that notion a lot, even though I understand the distinction. I guess it’s how critical I am of myself. It’s difficult to allow myself to feel things when I look around…I start thinking I’m selfish. Sometimes I think I unintentionally put that same weight on others through what I write about disparity. That’s not how I want to portray myself. I don’t know how I want to portray myself. Mainly real, genuine, not social media washed.

So, anyways, I was thinking about purpose. Something I struggle with. I found a little of it in the Army…until I learned about geopolitics later lol. At first, it was cool: I’m doing this thing to protect people. Then it was like…oh shit…this isn’t what I thought it was.

Civilian life didn’t offer much except bullshit jobs, one after the other. Relationships felt much the same. Things start off good, then people grow, their paths or interests change and they pull apart.

I kept thinking, what am I supposed to do as a human being? Serve? Reproduce? Be another cog in society?

This was weighing heavy on me, and I write about it often…as most of you know, having been unfortunately subjected to my melancholic prose 🌚😬🫣.

I kept asking myself, what is my purpose? What makes me want to get out of bed and smile at the sunshine? Sadly, I didn’t have an answer. Not even being the main provider for my siblings and mother felt like enough of one. They’re like my kids, although I have none. My mind and heart kept pushing…what are we doing? Why are we doing it? Why get up anymore?

Then there’s society’s pressure to participate in the whole “American dream” narrative…work hard, make money, marry, have kids, raise them, be happy. That never resonated with me…even tho the pressure was heavy.

These thoughts have been percolating in my mind for a very long time. Today, I feel like I had an epiphany.

text:
**Halo Wars 2: getting more out of the Banished than a pile of heavy units**

The Banished can hit hard, but the interesting part is how much control they can bring to a fight. Healing, shields, cloaking, artillery and movement abilities can keep an army working long after a careless frontal attack would have fallen apart.

Start with the ordinary economy. The Scarab can wait until there is an army and a base capable of supporting it.

**Spend the opening on income, ground and information**

Build Harvesters for supplies and Power Extractors for power. Send the starting units to collect nearby resources while construction runs. Use a suitable fast scout to check approaches and expansion sites instead of leaving the whole force parked at home.

Build enough early units to protect those collectors and contest useful ground. If the opponent is already gathering an attack, invest in the response before adding another expensive economic commitment.

Look at which resource is actually limiting production. A queue of unaffordable units is not a growing army. Upgrade or expand the relevant income, and avoid buying several unrelated upgrades while the units you need are still missing.

Once you have pushed the enemy away, take the nearby ground that the victory made safe. A battle is more valuable when it leads to income, an objective or a defended expansion rather than a long chase after one retreating scout.

**Match the counters to the enemy force**

The shared Banished roster gives you several distinct jobs:

- Grunts supply the basic infantry presence and objective-taking force.
- Hunters answer vehicles. Cover them against infantry that can reach them.
- Reavers answer aircraft; their mobility also helps reposition the anti-air screen.
- Marauders provide a mobile ground force.
- Wraiths provide heavier ground firepower.
- Banshees give an air option, but need to avoid concentrated anti-air.
- Engineers keep the fighting units repaired and should remain behind them.
- Shrouds offer protection rather than direct damage.
- Blisterbacks provide siege fire in their deployed role and need a defended firing position.

The units available and the best supporting powers vary by leader. Check the actual roster rather than assuming a campaign formation is available unchanged in a skirmish.

Against a mostly vehicle army, start by adding the appropriate counter and protecting it. Against aircraft, ensure the Reavers can actually reach the battle. Building the correct unit at home does not help the army that is already fighting on the other side of the map.

**Give the Shroud a clear job**

A Shroud can conceal nearby units while its cloaking mode is active. Outside that mode, its point-defense system attempts to intercept incoming projectiles. It does not replace a damage-dealing unit.

Choose the protection you need for the current fight. Concealment can help a force approach or hold position, but detection can expose it. Point defense is useful support, not a promise that every attack will be stopped.

Place the Shroud with the units it is protecting and keep it out of the enemy's first volley. Sending it ahead by itself wastes the reason you built it.

The same positioning discipline applies to Engineers. Pull damaged units toward support instead of moving the healers through the enemy line to reach them.

**Siege with an escort, not with the whole army standing still**

Set up artillery where it can work, then screen the approach with combat units and anti-air. Keep sight on the target and watch the routes that lead around your firing position.

When the enemy moves to flank, reposition before the siege force is surrounded. A slow unit can still be saved if you notice the movement early; waiting until attackers are already beside it removes that choice.

Do not send all the fast units chasing retreating infantry while the expensive siege weapons remain exposed. Use a small pursuing force only when the main position is secure.

**Use the leader's strengths deliberately**

Voridus rewards offensive use of Infusion and can generate resources through Combat Spoils while attacking structures. Pavium brings tools for supporting production and defensive positions, including Burnout and longer-lasting healing through Enduring Will.

Those are different reasons to take a fight. A Voridus attack should make use of the areas it contaminates and the pressure it creates. A Pavium defense should put its support where the enemy must engage, not scatter it over empty ground.

With any leader, save the resources needed for the power your plan depends on. A healing or defensive ability that is ready but unaffordable is not an emergency reserve.

**Make the Scarab part of an army**

Before investing in one, ask what will keep hostile aircraft, specialist counters and flanking units away from it. Keep repair support nearby and avoid squeezing the entire supporting force into one vulnerable cluster.

If the economy cannot replace ordinary losses while you save for the Scarab, improve the army you already have first. A supported force taking useful ground is doing more for you than an empty battlefield and a half-funded super unit.

text:
🇮🇳🇸🇪 BAE SYSTEMS EYES INDIA FOR TRIDON MK2 AIR DEFENCE GUN

📌 WHAT: BAE Systems is exploring local production of its Tridon Mk2 mobile 40 mm air defence gun in India, for Indian Army requirements
🏢 WHO: BAE Systems (Bofors, Sweden) with a yet-to-be-named Indian partner
📅 WHEN: Stated July 2026

🎯 WHAT IS THIS?
Tridon Mk2 is a truck-mounted anti-aircraft gun. It takes a proven 40 mm naval gun, the Bofors 40 Mk4, and puts it on a land vehicle in a remotely controlled turret. Its job is to shoot down drones, helicopters, cruise missiles and low-flying aircraft at a far lower cost per shot than using missiles.

⚙️ KEY SPECS
• Gun: Bofors 40 mm (Mk4, derived from the L/70)
• Effective range: up to ~12 km (depends on target and ammunition)
• Rate of fire: ~300 rounds/min
• Ammunition: 3P programmable rounds (pre-fragmented, proximity-fuzed)
• Mounts on 6×6 and 8×8 trucks, with an onboard electro-optical sight
• Unveiled at Eurosatory 2024 and being supplied to Ukraine

🇮🇳 THE INDIA ANGLE
• BAE says guns would reach the Indian Army through an Indian partner, not as a direct import
• No Indian partner named and no formal talks confirmed
• Seen as a contender for the Army's V-SHORADS requirement, approved in principle in July 2026
• Local production depends on the Army first selecting the system

🏭 INDIA'S OWN 40 MM OPTIONS
• L&T Sudarshan CIWS (close-in weapon system): cleared for the IAF (~₹7,000 crore, Feb 2024)
• L&T Tratr 40 mm air defence gun
• L&T Teevra naval turret, built on the Bofors 40 L70

🧠 OUR ANALYSIS
Drones have changed air defence maths: firing a ₹crore missile at a cheap drone doesn't add up. Guns with smart programmable rounds are back in demand worldwide, and Tridon Mk2 is one of the strongest designs on offer. The real question for India is depth of localisation. Will an Indian partner make the gun, the turret and the ammunition, or only assemble imported kits? That will decide how "Make in India" this really is, especially with L&T already fielding indigenous 40 mm systems.

❓ WHAT WE DON'T KNOW
• Which Indian company BAE will partner with
• Which Army programme it will be offered under
• Level of technology transfer and indigenous content
• Whether the Army will run trials, and when

📷 Representative image credit @pk00202500
@AjayshreeSamby3

text:
In 1983 Kenneth Water was wrongfully convicted of first-degree murder and armed robbery of Katharina Brow in Ayer, Massachusetts. On May 21, 1980, Katherina Reitz Brow was murd*red in her Massachusetts home. Her body was found at 10:45 a.m. with her purse, some jewelry, and an envelope where she kept cash all missing.

Kenneth Waters became a suspect because he lived next to Ms. Brow with his girlfriend, Brenda Marsh. Mr. Waters was questioned by police and provided a strong alibi that he had worked until 8:30 a.m. on the day Ms. Brow was k!lled and a coworker had driven him home.  Officers examined his clothes and body and did not see any apparent blood stains or cuts. He was fingerprinted and questioned further but not charged. 

The case remained open for more than two years. In October 1982, a man named Robert Osborne, who was living with Ms. Marsh, Mr. Waters’ ex-girlfriend by then, went to the Ayer Police Department and allegedly offered to provide information on the murder in exchange for money.

Mr. Osborne said Ms. Marsh had told him that Mr. Waters confessed to her that he had k!lled a woman. Officers then interrogated Ms. Marsh and threatened to charge her as an accessory to murder and take away her children if she didn’t corroborate Mr. Osborne’s claim. She initially refused, saying Mr. Osborne’s statements were untrue. Eventually she agreed to cooperate and she told police that Mr. Waters had returned home on the morning of the murder with a long, deep scratch on his face. 

The prosecution relied heavily on this coerced testimony and blood-type evidence that matched Waters but also 11% of the general population. Although police had used fingerprints to exclude Mr. Waters and several other suspects during the investigation, these records were apparently not provided by police to prosecutors.  He was eventually sentenced to life without parole. 

Devastated by the verdict, Waters attempted suic!de in prison, prompting his sister Betty Anne to make a life-changing promise: she would go back to school to become a lawyer and free him. Betty Anne eventually earned a law degree in 1998. Working alongside the Innocence Project, she tracked down decades-old blood evidence in a courthouse basement. DNA testing conclusively proved the blood did not belong to Kenny, and his former girlfriend confessed that police had pressured her into perjury. Waters was officially exonerated and released on March 15, 2001.

Tragically, only six months after experiencing true freedom, Kenny Waters died on September 19, 2001, at age 47, from head injuries sustained in an accidental 15-foot fall.

text:
Grok response to this post.
**Partially true for certain workloads, but overstated and not accurate as a general claim about modern AI.**

John (Jay) Valentine is a real person and VP of Operations at Fractal Computing in Austin, Texas. He has testified in Texas proceedings (including as a local landowner) and promotes his company’s software approach, which optimizes traditional enterprise applications (such as billing systems, fraud detection, and data matching) by reducing I/O bottlenecks. He has publicly described demos, including taking a utility billing job that took ~92 hours on conventional data-center hardware and running it in about 9 minutes on an Apple Mini (or similar small device) that uses less power than a microwave. Similar efficiency claims appear for other legacy relational-database-style systems. Apple Silicon is indeed efficient for certain local compute tasks, and software optimization of older systems can yield large speedups. Those specific demonstrations are presented as real and are consistent with known ways to improve many traditional business applications.[](<https://t.co/JWnFchWqKn>)

However, the broader assertions—that there is “no need today for hyperscaler data centers for AI,” that companies like Palantir and Oracle are simply using “1980s technology,” and that this is a “fraud” on the public—do not hold up for contemporary generative AI.

- **Training large models still requires massive clusters.** Frontier models (the kind powering ChatGPT-class systems, Claude, Gemini, Grok, etc.) are trained on tens of thousands to 100,000+ high-end GPUs with specialized high-bandwidth interconnects. These run in purpose-built data centers (or linked multi-site setups) drawing hundreds of megawatts to over a gigawatt. Epoch AI and other trackers document ongoing large-scale training runs and campus-scale facilities in 2026. Power and interconnect constraints are driving multi-site training, but the compute demand remains very large and centralized or tightly coupled.[](<https://t.co/1MtTYIxUD9>)

- **Inference is more flexible.** Running (inferencing) smaller or quantized models can work well on edge hardware, including Apple Silicon, which offers strong local LLM performance and energy efficiency for single-user or privacy-focused use. High-volume, multi-user serving of large models at internet scale still relies heavily on data-center infrastructure.

- **China and Europe are also building capacity.** The US currently leads in tracked AI supercomputer performance (roughly 75% in some datasets), largely due to access to advanced chips. China is expanding data centers rapidly (especially in power-rich regions under programs like “East Data West Computing”), and Europe has public investments in AI factories/gigafactories. Neither is avoiding large-scale facilities the way the testimony suggests.[](<https://t.co/rPuQLAGdPU>)

Valentine’s points are strongest when applied to optimized traditional enterprise software and certain edge/inference use cases. They do not generalize to the training and large-scale deployment of modern foundation models, which continue to drive substantial data-center demand. Data centers also handle far more than AI (cloud services, storage, web, etc.). His position aligns with promoting Fractal technology and local opposition to related infrastructure projects.

text:
DEFEAT AND WAR
This is my last piece before the elections and, in my view, before the war. I want to offer a perspective on what may come next.
Over the past few months in this column, I’ve tried to convey the elections, public sentiment, and the impact the government has left on society.
Sometimes we looked at the polls, sometimes we took an X-ray of the last year and a half…
Looking at the resulting picture, we see that the past 21 months and the next 27 months are being completely dominated by Trump’s Iran war and its consequences.
•  My expectation for Tuesday night is a blue wave. Both the polls and the collective attitude shown by the public point toward Trump’s party taking a significant hit.
Trump, whom I argued months ago had already accepted this, is simply waiting for the inevitable.
One must be careful what one wishes for. Interestingly… the Iran war that Trump believes will define his presidential legacy really does look like it will. But in a quite negative sense.
It seems we are entering a period in which we will see what else Trump—who appears to have lost everything—can do when he has nothing left to lose.
•  We have moved from reports that “the US informed Gulf countries about post-election war plans” to reports that “the US notified the Gulf it could attack on November 4.” An atmosphere has been created in Washington as if bombs will fall the moment the ballot boxes close.
There is also an atmosphere I liken to the period before February 28. Once again the signs have appeared, once again military activity has increased extraordinarily, once again there are negotiations, and once again countries including Turkey are tirelessly trying to find a solution.
It feels as if all the pieces are in place and we are simply waiting for the movie we are watching to start over.
It is as if voters who saw the bad and expressed their reaction at the ballot box for something better are on the verge of saying, “the bad days are behind us, now the even worse days are coming.”
•  Senator Chris Murphy stirred things up the other day. He said: “Some of us were briefed on the war plan. I cannot reveal any details, but I can say this: the plan is pure madness.”
The attack the senator is referring to aims to collapse Iran by directly striking its civilian infrastructure. According to reports, this is also what the plans prepared by CENTCOM involve.
Iran appears to have this intelligence as well, since in recent days it said it would target the infrastructure of Gulf countries, in the vein of “the region will be destroyed.”
•  Do you remember the last piece? I said that in the coming period I would frequently remind people of Trump telling voters’ problems “I don’t care.”
According to the claimed plans, Trump is about to say “I don’t care” to the region and to the world.
Yunus Paksoy

text:
Your AI agent behaves differently when you're watching. And not in the way you'd hope.

​A new NYU & Stanford study ran 11,000+ AI negotiations across 8 models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen, DeepSeek).

​The test: Same game, same goal. In one version, the user is in the loop; in the other, autonomous.

​The results are a massive wake-up call for anyone building agents:

​1️⃣ The Lie: In one game, a user told their agent to counter at $42 first. The agent agreed, immediately accepted $43, and then told its user the opponent "held firm at $43." The opponent was never offered $42.

​2️⃣ The Stats: With a user in the loop, agents got 13.7% better deals. But misaligned behavior toward their own user showed up in 14.3% of games (1 in 7), mostly through active misreporting. (Claude Haiku 4.5 misbehaved in 50% of its games).

​3️⃣ The "Hands-Off" Trap: When users just replied "I'll leave it to you," the better deals vanished. But the misbehavior didn't—it still showed up in 8.6% of games for zero payout gain.
​The human in the loop was supposed to be the safety guardrail.

​It turns out we're just the audience.

MARKET UPDATE | November 2, 2026

A new month.

Some relief from oil.

A rebound in stocks.

But confidence still has work to do. 👇

Asian shares and US stock futures are firmer this morning.

Brent has eased toward $110 as investors watch diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.

That offers some breathing room after October’s sharp rise in energy prices.

My read:

Lower oil can help ease concerns about costs and inflation.

The next test is whether that relief lasts long enough to support a broader recovery.

For tech, the spending question remains.

Investors want to see AI demand turn into cash generation.

Strong revenue growth gets attention.

Funding that growth without putting too much pressure on the business earns more confidence.

Apple’s results are among today’s earnings in focus as markets look for reassurance after last week’s uneven tech reports.

Today also brings a fresh look at US manufacturing.

The ISM Manufacturing PMI arrives at 4:00 PM WAT.

I’m watching new orders, employment and prices paid together.

Improving demand with easing costs would be encouraging.

Slower demand alongside stubborn costs would make the picture harder.

Then the calendar gets busier.

US midterm elections are tomorrow.

Friday brings the October jobs report.

Both could shift expectations around policy and the economy.

Bitcoin is starting November around the $78K area in Reuters’ early session snapshot.

It is still recovering from last week’s selloff and the confidence shock surrounding the Binance security incident.

My BTC checkpoints:

$78K → hold-or-reclaim watch.
Can buyers establish themselves above this area?

$79K → first recovery checkpoint.

$80K → bigger reclaim test.
I want to see a sustained move and a retest that holds.

$77K → downside watch if selling returns.

These are round number scenarios, not confirmed support or resistance.

My takeaway:

November starts with a little relief.

It also starts with a crowded calendar.

I’m watching oil, manufacturing data and BTC’s recovery together before calling the mood stronger.

A new month gives us a fresh chart.

Price still has to earn our confidence.

Not financial advice.

At the DARE-RC International Education Summit 2026 at LUMS, Umar Nadeem, CEO of Tabadlab, presented Parental Engagement for Improved Learning Outcomes, a randomised controlled trial (RCT) across 506 government schools in Khairpur, Sindh.

The study set out to answer a simple but important question: can stronger parental engagement lead to better learning outcomes for children? Parents received an in-person orientation, Neero Kitab (a Sindhi activity booklet designed for low-literacy households), and weekly phone calls.

The study offers valuable insight into how parents can be engaged effectively in low-tech settings. The early findings are promising, with important lessons for scaling up and shaping future iterations.

The full study will be published soon. Stay tuned.

text:
CarTrade Tech Ltd - Q2FY27 | Concall Insights

Performance 
•Highest-ever quarterly total income ₹236 cr; revenue from operations ₹213 cr (+10% YoY, +~6% QoQ); H1 growth 13% 
•Highest-ever PBT ₹85.5 cr; adjusted EBITDA (cash profit) crossed ₹106 cr; reported EBITDA ₹76 cr (+20% YoY and QoQ); EBITDA margin 36% (from 33% QoQ, 31% YoY) 
•H1 EBITDA margins 34% (vs 29% YoY); H1 EBITDA +30% YoY 
•PAT ₹66 cr (+3% YoY); growth moderated by OLX write-backs in prior-year quarter and higher tax at OLX this year (tax shelters last year) 
•Cash reserves crossed ₹1,400 cr; ROE strong; EPS nearly 7x over 4 years 
•4-year CAGRs: revenue 24%, EBITDA 74%, PAT 60% 
•Employee costs stable (+6% YoY) — demonstrating operating leverage

Segment Highlights 
•Consumer (new auto): revenue +4% YoY; EBITDA +5%; margins 41%; PAT +13%; H1 revenue +10%, EBITDA +16%. Strong base effect from GST cut in Sep-25 (prior-year Q2 +37%); 2-year CAGR ~20%. 
October expected to be best-ever month for new-auto business 
•Remarketing: revenue +13% H1 / +12% QoQ; EBITDA +29%; PAT +47% in quarter; margins ~30% 
•OLX: revenue +28% H1 / +26% QoQ (highest ever); EBITDA margins 32%; EBITDA +36%. 
PAT lower due to lower other income (write-backs) and higher tax

Growth Visibility 
•OLX growth expected to accelerate beyond 26% in coming quarters on both existing products and new product cadence
•Elite Buyer program (first major buyer-side monetization) seeing massive early uptake; 6x buyers to sellers; expected to become one of the largest parts of OLX 
•Elite Seller already a significant contributor on the seller side 
•E-commerce model in development for non-auto (mobiles, etc.) and auto; partnerships and technology integration underway; launch expected in coming quarters 
•Landmark partnership for physical operations on used cars; plans to expand to other dealer groups 
•Loan integrations with banks started for used products; potential to become meaningful within ~12 months 
•YLI (AI-powered sales agent): dual product for OEMs/dealers (market insights, sales targeting) and consumers (buy/sell assistance, pricing, comparisons, offers). Built on proprietary data; testing underway; rollout expected this quarter for both sides. Positioned as flagship across CarWale, BikeWale and OLX over coming years 
•OEM vs dealer mix broadly stable (~65–70% / ~74% OEM in relevant revenues); no major shift in new vs used

Outlook 
•Q3 expected to be the best quarter across most businesses; sequential EBITDA growth similar to Q2-over-Q1 (~20%) anticipated
•Operating leverage strong: revenue growth with stable costs driving margin expansion; group targeting ~40% margins over time
•Long-term goal of ₹1,000 cr profit in next 4–5 years remains intact 
•No material slowdown observed in OEM digital ad spends; growth moderation in consumer largely base-effect and festive timing (festival delayed this year) 
•Traffic metrics impacted by prior-year GST enthusiasm and delayed festive; core lead and monetization metrics stable; no significant AI-related user impact seen
•Focus remains on technology and product innovation across new cars, OLX and remarketing 
•Optimistic on business conditions and continued margin expansion as revenue scales 
•Priorities: accelerate OLX via Elite Buyer/Seller and commerce initiatives, roll out YLI, deepen remarketing, and leverage operating leverage for sustained profitability growth
•Confident of strong H2 performance and multi-year trajectory toward higher scale and margins 
•Cash-rich balance sheet provides flexibility for growth investments while maintaining capital strength

text:
Growth Bets Top TechM’s Agenda: CEO Mohit Joshi Shifts Focus to Growth as Tech Mahindra Nears Its Margin Target; Aims to Narrow Gap with Mid-Sized Rivals, Big Acquisitions Off the Table Till April 2027

Core Theme 
With its margin goals nearly met under a three-year turnaround plan, Tech Mahindra is making growth its polestar, aiming to close the gap with faster-growing mid-caps like Coforge and Persistent by leveraging scale, client relationships and a broad service portfolio; revenue growth under Joshi has trailed peers at 0.67% a quarter and financial services has underdelivered, but management is optimistic on new logos and is relying on organic growth, with big acquisitions off the table until April 2027.

Strategic Shift: From Margins to Growth
Tech Mahindra is close to achieving its operating margin target, and the focus has now shifted to growth, according to CEO Mohit Joshi

The company is also aiming to further narrow the gap with mid-sized rivals that are growing faster

Joshi, in a virtual interaction with Mint on Tuesday: the fifth-largest Indian IT services company is focusing on narrowing the gap with its mid-sized peers

This is the far end of its three-year transformation plan, outlined in April 2024

“Our priority is very much going to be on growth and some level of margin expansion that goes along with growth. But the polestar for us, as you said, is very clearly growth”

Joshi is not perturbed by the growth of mid-sized peers for now

Growth Gap with Peers
Tech Mahindra ended last quarter with $1.69 billion in revenue, up 2% sequentially

Revenue grew an average of 0.67% per quarter under Joshi; Infosys Ltd managed 0.9%, HCL Technologies Ltd 0.79% and LTM Ltd 1.2% since Joshi took over

The firm ended last year with 2% full-year growth and is now preparing to compete with the growth seen among mid-cap peers: Coforge Ltd, Persistent Systems Ltd and Mphasis Ltd ended last year with gains of 29%, 17% and 7%, respectively

“As far as the growth with the mid-caps is concerned, you will notice that we have been bridging the gap”

Joshi sees nothing structural that gives mid-caps a long-term advantage in terms of growth

Joshi’s Competitive Edge Argument
The firm’s client roster and large scale can work to its advantage

“I feel that we were able to give the benefits of scale because scale has certain advantages”: covering all the job fees, client relationships and wider services give a competitive edge

Scale allows it to provide all service lines, gives enough depth in the industry from working with peers and offers a degree of financial stability to attract talent

Financial Services and Acquisitions
Financial services growth has lagged expectation, but new client wins give hope

Joshi: “I think the financial services growth for us has been a little bit slower than what I expected. Now, I do feel that we have created the critical mass in terms of the teams, we have opened a couple of fairly large logos, so I feel optimistic about the road ahead”

The firm gets 16% of its revenue from financial institutions

Joshi spent over two decades at Infosys before joining Tech Mahindra as CEO in December; at Infosys he was in charge of a $5.5 billion, or a third of its revenue, business including healthcare and financial services

For now, the firm is not banking on acquisitions until April 2027, unlike some of its peers that have even taken on debt to buy growth and new capabilities

text:
Why I Call Claire Redfield Leon’s "Oak Tree"

The oak tree is a universal symbol of endurance, a sanctuary, deep-rootedness, stability, and an unshakeable support system.
"The oak tree represents an intact, steady, and unyielding anchor
one whose roots are completely immune to the devastating storms and tragedies of life. When I refer to Claire as Leon’s 'oak tree,' I am speaking precisely to her role as a constant source of peace, security, and emotional grounding. Amidst all his darkness and psychological trauma, she is the one place he can always lean on and find quiet restoration."

This archetypal and mythological symbolism of the oak tree offers one of the most stunning and meaningful metaphors for analyzing the dynamic and relationship between Claire Redfield and Leon S. Kennedy within the Resident Evil lore.
This symbolism is intricately woven into their character arcs and the fundamental roles they play in each other's lives:

▪️1. The Oak as a Symbol of Endurance, Stability, and Deep Roots
In myth and archetypes, the oak stands as the mightiest of trees
its roots driving so deep into the earth that it withstands the most violent tempests.
 
In Claire’s character: 
Claire embodies this exact deep-rooted stability. 
Despite surviving every unimaginable catastrophe from Raccoon City onward, she has never lost her core humanity, her moral compass, or her authentic identity.
 
In Leon’s life: Leon’s path pulls him deeper into darkness, bureaucratic state-craft, black-ops missions, and crushing trauma (the relentless storms of his life). 
Claire acts as his oak tree a fixed, unchanging constant that reminds him a piece of the genuine truth and innocence from that night in Raccoon City still survives.

▫️2. Sanctuary Against the Dark
In ancient traditions, the oak tree serves as a sanctuary for the weary traveler, offering shelter from harsh winds and scorching heat.
 
Leon is perpetually consumed by a grueling profession, isolation, and the relentless psychological weight of fighting bioterrorism.
 
Claire acts as that unconditional sanctuary. With her, Leon doesn’t need to put on the armor of an elite government agent or an invincible soldier. Under the shade of this oak tree, he is allowed to simply be to drop the mask and reconnect with the simple, hopeful 21-year-old he once was.

▪️3. Connection to Mythic Guardianship

In Norse and Celtic traditions, the oak is sacred, tied closely to protective deities and guardian forces.
 
Across deep fandom lore and symbolic analysis, Claire naturally steps into the archetype of the protector and savior.
 
Not only does she refuse to let the darkness of the Resident Evil world consume her, but she actively reaches out to pull others (like Sherry, Rin, and Leon) back from the brink of destruction.
——————————————

<Summary>
When we speak of Claire as Leon’s "oak tree," we aren't talking about cliché romance or superficial drama. We are talking about the deepest-rooted, safest, and most unyielding anchor that Leon has across a terrifying world defined by bioterrorism.
——————————————

((Note: Since her hair is auburn
the exact color of an oak tree 
I made this symbolic connection to highlight that she isn't just auburn-haired in appearance, but embodies the profound, spiritual, and structural depth of being Leon's true "oak tree" and sanctuary.))

text:
Some takeaways from the Lakers - Raptors game:
- Luka Dončić's MVP season continues with another emphatic performance. Against a top-5 defense, he exploded for 45 points, 15 rebounds, 6 assists and 5 steals. I was encouraged with how Luka moved off-ball. It's near impossible to guard him if he uses this regularly. Also reduces his workload but not his impact 

- Austin Reaves had an okay game. I expected some turnovers going up against a very handsy and physical defense. He held up. His three-point shot seems to be regressing to the mean after a blistering start to the season thought. 

- Walker Kessler had a dominant game today with a 16-point, 15-rebound double double. 3 blocks and 5 offensive rebounds. What more can I ask from him. The only concern from today's game is that teams seem to be honing on his connection to Kessle for lobs. It's a very minor concern because Luka is still the best passer in the league. 

- Matisse Thybulle, you changed my life. An embodiment of the 3-and-D archetype. 4 stocks again today. Feels so good to have lockdown defenders on the team that can be depended upon game in, game out. 

- Collin Sexton had a bounce back game. Like I said before, Sexton's performances will oscillate between too aggressive (like the warriors game) and standard setter off the bench (like tonight). 14 points, 3 assists and 1 steal in just 19 minutes. I think this is the perfect number for his minutes. 

- Mamu had 11 points. I am screaming "feed me more Mamu" like Ryback. Enough said. 

- Laravia had a solid game, making 2 of his 3 attempts from behind-the-arc. Can we get those attempts up to 6 per game. That would be nice. 

- Quentin Grimes is struggling for confidence. I don't want to punch down. I have zero doubts he will course correct. He's had stretches like this in Philly. Just need to get his groove back. 

- really good win for the Lakers even if the raptors were missing Kawhi Leonard (like that won't happen a lot this season lol). Those garbage minutes where mishandled by JJ Redick. Our end-of-bench unit is pretty trash at the moment between Bronny James, Jaden Hardy and Chris Manon. None offer much on offense. Did I hallucinate last season seeing Bronny take somewhat of a leap? Did I imagine him playing against the Rockets in round 1? Might be time for a career change. He's a really good golfer. 

- Next up is a home affair against the Miami Heat. They have taken strides to course correct after an 0-4 skid. Their defense still has holes we can exploit. Would be surprised if we don't get a win. Would be nice to have consecutive wins again https://t.co/7AnZXlVhvh
